item.title: Thing of Things AI use policy
item.description: dynomight recently wrote an article calling for bloggers to state publicly whether and how they use AI
item.content:encoded:
dynomight recently wrote an article calling for bloggers to state publicly whether and how they use AI:

I bring this up because I’m worried that blogs are heading into a sort of lemon market. You’ve surely had the experience of reading an essay only to slowly become dismayed as you realize it was AI-written. What’s the equilibrium? I expect that some people have already cut back on reading essays, at least from non-established authors. Over time, I expect this will lead to fewer humans writing essays, further increasing the density of AI-generated content, driving more people to cut back on reading, et cetera. This is bad because blogs are good.

As that cycle turns, social norms are also changing. Cast your mind back to the old world, five years ago. At that time, if you had started a blog and posted AI-generated essays without telling anyone, I’m reasonably certain that would have been considered a dick move. (Future generations will marvel.) But today, the largest corporations appear to do that all the time. There’s incredible momentum towards a world where AI can be used anywhere, for any purpose, with no disclosure, and that’s fine.

But it is fine! At this point, trying to bully people into proactive disclosure is just a tax on honesty / consciousness / integrity. Instead, I suggest we agree that arbitrary usage is, by default, fine. Instead, let’s work at the other end: If you have chosen to impose limits on your AI usage, then state those limits publicly. If you’re human, tell me...

I think this is a good idea so I’m doing it.

Like dynomight, I will “guarantee that every word I post here is the product of me physically hitting keys with my fingers. The only exceptions would be quotes from other humans or something that’s clearly labeled as an AI output.”1

The most common way I use AI when writing posts is as an advanced search engine and/or thesaurus: I ask questions like “Synonyms for ‘safe’ in the sense of being free from danger?” or “What are some events that have a 1% probability?” or “what’s the word for the thing where if a small interest group would be helped a lot by a policy, and everyone else would be harmed a tiny bit by that policy, the policy is more likely to get passed because none of the people harmed care enough to protest?” I do this probably three or four times a post.

I use AIs to check facts in blog posts: “there are definitely Chinese temples that are critically acclaimed by architects, right?”, “can you give an example of an extremely niche kind of quantitative trading someone might specialize in?”, “what’s a hemiellipsoid body? Please explain to me like I’m five.” I usually independently fact-check anything the AI tells me; I ask it for sources and then read the sources myself, or I google keywords and follow up with a reliable source. Occasionally I don’t bother—for example, if the fact is supposed to add color to an example or a joke, rather than being information I expect people to rely on.

I use AIs regularly to find papers for lit reviews, if I’m writing a post that requires a lit review, instead of digging through Google Scholar and paper citations myself. When I’m doing a literature review post, I read all the papers myself, rather than relying on an AI summary.2 I may occasionally ask AIs to explain aspects of a paper I don’t understand.

I have yet to use Claude Code to analyze data, but I expect I will in the future. When using Claude Code to analyze data, I will thoroughly look over the code to make sure that I understand what all of it is doing and that I approve. One of my beta readers doubts my claim here because Claude Code produces so much code that it is impractical to check all the data analysis code manually, but I would much rather write my own data analysis code than publish data analysis I don’t understand and might not stand by.

Probably I would use AIs to generate tables and graphs, if I ever put tables and graphs in my Substack, which I don’t because I’m not a visual thinker.

I don’t use AIs for editing nonfiction. Frankly, I don’t edit my nonfiction that much at all. At least 40% of the time you guys are reading my unedited first drafts.

I don’t use AIs for brainstorming blog posts because it feels icky. I want to develop my ideas through getting in arguments on Discord forthright and rational debate with people I respect, the way Socrates intended. I want to get several different perspectives on a nascent idea, and modern AIs can only give me one perspective. Besides, “arguing with people in a way that might become a blog post” is like 15% of my social interaction. This is the stance that is least likely to change, at least before we build a Dyson sphere out of Mercury.

1

Can we call this the Dynomight Pledge?

2

Sometimes this is a heroic act of self-sacrifice.

item.title: Christians and effective altruism
item.description: I. As with the last time I reviewed an effective altruism book, I am using All The Lives You Can Change as a spur to write a barely related essay.
item.content:encoded:
I.

As with the last time I reviewed an effective altruism book, I am using All The Lives You Can Change as a spur to write a barely related essay. And as with the last time I reviewed an effective altruism book, I will open the piece by explaining who should read this book.

All The Lives You Can Change is an introduction to effective altruist ideas aimed at Christian readers.1 If you read this Substack or otherwise participate in the effective altruist community, even if you’re a Christian, it will have almost no new information for you. However, if you’d enjoy reading about Badass Christians of the Past, you might want to get a copy and skip past all the introduction to EA stuff to read more about badass Christians. (I particularly recommend Oliver’s Story, page 35.)

However, as an introduction to effective altruist thought, All The Lives You Can Change seems unobjectionable. It covers the basic topics in an accessible way. I don’t know whether the authors master the ingroup signifiers of Protestantism.2 But in general it seems like a good book to give to friends and family who are devout (Protestant) Christians and whom you think would be interested in effective altruism if it were presented to them properly, or who want to know about that effective altruism stuff you spend all your time doing. It also seems like potentially an interesting read for a church book group, if you’re an effective altruist Christian yourself who wants to introduce the ideas of effective altruism to your church.

II.

The entire time I was reading this book I was going: C A U S E P R I O R I T I Z A T I O N

Fundamentally, effective altruism comes from a secular set of assumptions. If you genuinely believe that an all-good God governs the universe, that suggests that many effective altruist assumptions are mistaken. In a secular context, like the Effective Altruism Forum, arguments should be made from secular principles. But in a religious context like All The Lives You Can Change, I really want to see rigorous cause prioritization work coming from a Christian worldview.

Global health is probably the area where Christians and secular effective altruists agree most. All The Lives You Can Change does a nice job highlighting the role of care for the poor in Scripture and Tradition (or whatever the Protestant equivalent of Scripture and Tradition is). Fundamentally, God has commanded Christians to feed the hungry and clothe the naked and look after the sick, and GiveWell is the best source of information about how to do that efficiently (especially now that they’ve expanded into livelihoods research).

All The Lives You Can Change addresses animal welfare but not in very much detail: it points out that there are a lot of farmed animals, and that many farmed animals are horrifically mistreated. But I’d like to see a more detailed discussion of animal welfare from a Christian perspective, perhaps along the lines of Matthew Scully’s Dominion, which argues that God granting humans dominion over animals actually requires us to treat animals with mercy and stewardship.

From a secular perspective, humans are on a spectrum with animals: they suffer and feel joy the same way we do. Secular animal advocates emphasize that, because animals are similar to humans, they have the same rights humans do to be protected from unnecessary suffering or from exploitation. But from a Christian perspective, humans and animals are fundamentally different, because only humans have souls and were made in the image of God. You can be a Christian and advocate for animal welfare. But Christians come at animal advocacy from a different perspective than non-Christians, and I wanted to see that explored more thoroughly.

All The Lives You Can Change falters when it addresses longtermist cause areas, such as AI safety. From a Christian perspective, you know exactly how humanity is going to end, and it isn’t “an AI released a bioengineereed pandemic because it was afraid we would try to turn it off.” Furthermore, to Christians, the end of humanity as presently conceived isn’t the destruction of all value, the way it is for secular people; to the contrary, it’s the beginning of the world to come, a period of literally infinite goodness.3

Furthermore, Christians almost all believe in objective morality. From a secular perspective, AI alignment is hard, because you’re trying to specify one complicated set of goals that isn’t any different from nearby complicated sets of goals that would result in disaster. But from a Christian perspective, the correct goals for AIs to have are different from other goals, because morality is a fact about the universe and not a fact about human minds. Under a Christian worldview, AI alignment is likely substantially easier than it is under secular worldviews.

Even from a Christian perspective, AI is a powerful technology, and some people ought to devote their careers to ensuring it goes well. But most people who work on AI safety believe that teaching an AI to want safe things is extremely difficult, and if we fail at it then all humans might die, and so destroy all value in the universe.4 If you don’t accept any of those three beliefs, the case that AI risk is overwhelmingly important is pretty weak.

A Christian longtermism likely looks very different from a secular longtermism. Christians probably ought to be more sympathetic to patient longtermism, and also more sympathetic to non-existential-risk-focused varieties of longtermism. As such, I’d expect a Christian longtermism to focus on movement building, global priorities research, and saving money to donate decades or centuries in the future—all proposals that look good under patient longtermism. Similarly, Christian longtermism would probably focus more on making the future better, and less on making sure that there’s a future at all: for example, to the extent that it addresses AI, Christian longtermism probably ought to focus on values lock-in and gradual disempowerment, rather than existential risk.

I also think a Christian longtermism should potentially focus on preserving the global church. One of the longest-lasting human institutions is the Christian church (specifically its Catholic and Orthodox strains). Guiding the church itself and ensuring its preservation seems like a crucial cause area for Christian longtermists.

Of course, if you believe existential risk is impossible and the future is inevitably going to be great, the case for longtermism itself—that is, the idea that one of our major moral priorities should be making sure the long-term future goes well—is much weaker. Longtermism is important to secular people because secular people believe the world isn’t guided by God’s providence. If it is, shaping the future yourself seems much less important!

All The Lives You Can Change, however, recommends a longtermism whose conclusions are pretty similar to the conclusions of secular effective altruists. Some of its arguments—that there might be a lot of people in the future, and that we tend to underweight the future—seem plausible. But it also says:

The theologian N. T. Wright argues that building just institutions, and attending to the needs of the world around us, is fully compatible with a belief in the end times. This is because the “new creation” should be understood as a fulfillment, rather than a replacement, of our efforts to build a better world. Our role in building this new creation may mean investing in institutions, policies, and actions that affect future generations; we should trust God to honor this good work, rather than see our long-term actions as futile.

what we don’t know is the mechanism by which humans are saved from extinction. It may be that God fulfills his plans through our actions; there is plenty of precedent for this in the Bible, from Mary’s obedience to Judas’s treachery... A Christian might very reasonably conclude that God is calling her to faithfully work to prevent human extinction, even if she trusts that such an extinction may never happen, and God may be using her to prevent that very outcome.

It’s not like these arguments are wrong, precisely. It’s just that they feel like the author first wrote “Christian effective altruists should prioritize the same longtermist cause areas secular effective altruists do” as their conclusion on the bottom of the page, and then filled in any argument that came to hand.

Certainly many Christians believe that Christians work to bring about the New Creation.5 But I’m not sure why that would mean preventing great power conflict or improving political institutions, instead of giving people malaria nets or fighting factory farming. Malaria and factory farming aren’t part of the New Creation either! The division being made here is one that makes sense from a secular perspective; if you want to make the argument that preventing great power conflict and improving political institutions are better ways of building the New Creation than preventing malaria and doing cage-free egg campaigns, you have to make that argument from Christian principles.

Similarly, “maybe God is using us as His tools to accomplish the inevitable continued existence of humanity” raises serious questions about causality and cluelessness. What’s the counterfactual here? If God is definitely not going to let humanity go extinct, wouldn’t the counterfactual impact of existential risk work be literally zero? Or maybe we’d be putting God in the position of making some kind of unfortunate tradeoff: maybe He brings about a civilizational collapse because that’s the only way to prevent a bioengineered pandemic that kills everyone. Does this suggest that we should focus on preventing existential risks that cause an unfortunate tradeoff for God (like bioengineered pandemics) over those that definitely don’t (God can simply make sure there aren’t any planetkiller asteroids around)?

If you accept the premise that you should do work with zero counterfactual impact because you might be God’s tool, the entire way effective altruists reason about effectiveness is caused into question. Developed-world doctors have a relatively small counterfactual impact, but maybe God chose you as His tool to perform amputations for reasons of His own. This argument saves existential risk work at the cost of effective altruism itself.

The section I found least convincing was the section on evangelism. From a Christian effective altruist perspective, Christian evangelism is extremely important. Like helping the poor, it is the subject of an explicit commandment from God (the Great Commission). In Christian theology, forming a personal relationship with God is the literal purpose of human existence. And—not to put too fine a point on it—the mainstream Christian belief is that non-Christians are risking a literal eternity of torture. Seems bad!

I agree that the Bible commands a portfolio approach where Christians both help the poor and do evangelism. Christians can’t accept the straightforward consequentialist argument that any risk of eternal torture outweighs any finite suffering in this life. The argument I’m most skeptical of is:

One view is that becoming a Christian is a spiritual process that is deeply personal. Many Christians throughout history have experienced it as a revelation or as God’s grace working in us, rather than us playing an active part in the process. Even if friends, family, authors, and pastors have supported our faith journeys, to many of us faith can feel more like God’s mysterious gift rather than an outcome that others have produced in us. Some denominations go even further and place the responsibility for conversion fully in God’s hands, such that entire revivals are the direct intervention of the Holy Spirit rather than the result of clever human strategizing about church growth.

Clearly, Christians have different models of conversion, but under all models, evangelism arguably works in a somewhat different way from providing food for the hungry or jabs for the unvaccinated. To put it crudely, there is less human agency and more divine agency. There is no button to press on a machine, much less predictability about outcomes, and it becomes harder to apply human models to maximize results.

This is primarily a point about tractability; it is not easy for us to control or guarantee conversions, and therefore difficult for us to adopt an “effective” approach to evangelism. However, there is also a point about division of labor. Since the Bible clearly indicates that the demands of the Christian life are more than just evangelism, including living our lives in certain ways and attending to the earthly needs of those around us, it is plausible that strategizing about saving souls on a macro level is more God’s job than ours.

But the exact argument used in favor of working on existential risk can be used in favor of evangelism: even if God wills that a particular person be saved, He might have chosen you as His tool to save them. And whether any particular person is saved is (clearly) far more in question than whether God would allow humanity to be unexpectedly driven extinct or whether the world to come is devoid of all value.

Besides, most effective altruist cause areas are hard to control or guarantee. Is evangelism really harder to collect evidence about than AI alignment, alternative protein development, the preservation of American democracy, or global priorities research? Under Christian premises, God is certainly particularly involved in conversions, but are we to assume that His involvement is qualitatively different than His involvement in malaria nets or cash transfers? Doesn’t God Himself have a special concern for the poor? Isn’t every human a subject of His special care, protection, guidance, and love?

Overall, I felt like I wanted significantly more thought about cause prioritization. A friend of mine, a serious Christian and serious effective altruist, has done her own cause prioritization work. Because she’s pro-life, she donates to the Against Malaria Foundation, which she believes to be the most cost-effective way to prevent miscarriages. And she considers healing the Great Schism to be potentially one of the top effective altruist cause areas. It’s this energy I wanted from All The Lives You Can Change, and it’s this energy I wasn’t getting.

Christianity is a set of fact claims, which imply different actions than the fact claims believed by the average atheist effective altruist. A Christian effective altruist’s cause prioritization shouldn’t look like an atheist effective altruist’s cause prioritization.

III.

The passage in All The Lives You Can Change that most stuck with me is:

The Christian message starts first and fully with affirming our weakness. It doesn’t start with us pulling ourselves together. It starts with acknowledging that the superpowers described in this book have been put into frail hands. And when we acknowledge this, God’s work can start...

since Christianity affirms our weakness while simultaneously affirming our infinite worth, the two must be compatible. God loves us—no matter what. His love is independent of whether we have much potential to make the world a better place, and of whether we make good use of this potential. Our impact and our worth are utterly independent from each other. You may be Norman Borlaug, whose actions fed billions—or you may be a random person in a small town struggling with failed relationships, addiction, and a slow-moving career. From God’s perspective, the two of you are equally fascinating, valuable, and infinitely worthy of his love...

affirming our weakness means, perhaps surprisingly, that we can aim high. How come? Because of grace; we don’t need to be overwhelmed by the gap between our ambition and our actions. In contrast, the secular world often finds it harder to acknowledge the chasm between our high ideals and our pitiful failures. And the secular response to this chasm can be to dial down our standards: Aren’t we pretty decent anyway, at least most of the time, and surely when compared to some of history’s true villains? Low standards feel like the only livable standards. But this is not the Christian route. Instead of watering down ideals, we can simply accept our shortcomings and rely on God’s grace to make the gap bearable.

Effective altruists like strength. More people than would like to admit the fact joined the effective altruism through reading Harry Potter and the Methods of Rationality, in which Harry James Potter-Evans-Verres famously says, “Every time someone cries out in prayer and I can’t answer, I feel guilty about not being God.”6

A lot of effective altruists, even those that joined the community in some more dignified manner, are sympathetic to Harry James Potter-Evans-Verres here. It feels like it ought to be possible to become better and fix everything. When I summarized effective altruism in three traits, one of them was ambition. Even once we’ve made our peace with not being able to solve any problem with a snap of our fingers, we like becoming more powerful, richer, better-connected, more intelligent, more diligent, more skilled, more able to shape the world to our will.

I’m not different here. My blog description, for a long time, has been “the nicest herrenmoralist”, which is the best compliment Scott Alexander ever gave me. To me, that means you ought to become brave and strong and talented and powerful, all that Nietzschean master morality stuff, and then you ought to use your courage and strength and talent and power not for self-aggrandizement but to make the world better.

“Every time someone cries out in prayer and I can’t answer, I feel guilty about not being God” is, for obvious reasons, less appealing to people who believe there is a literal God in His Heaven Whose hand is guiding the world with wisdom and love. Secular effective altruists tend to be deep atheists; the only people who can improve on the barbarity and suffering of the world we have been given are us, and since it is notably difficult to get “us” to do anything, that really means that the only person who can do anything about it is you.

But I’m still interested in the prospect of approaching effective altruism from a perspective of weakness. Heroic responsibility, ambition, herrenmoralism, and the rest all have the problem that they have nothing to say to you when you fail. Just git gud. If you can’t git gud, then idk you’re an NPC and Homer will allot half a metric foot to Achilles stabbing you with a spear.

And everyone is going to fail. For one thing, disease and depression and irreversible serious mistakes and errors of judgment and grief and aging are the human condition.7 But there’s a deeper thing here.

If you’re sufficiently ambitious, a version of the Peter Principle applies to your own life. If you reach your goals, you will raise your sights, which means that you will pursue more and more ambitious goals until you find a goal you can’t achieve. It might be “become the president of the United States”, it might be “get out of bed this morning”, but regardless your targets will rise to the level of your incompetence.

Since incompetence is an inevitable feature of the ambitious life, we ought to figure out some way to deal with it. And I think a good approach here does, in some sense, involve affirming our weakness. To an atheist, there isn’t a specific Person Who believes that you are fascinating, valuable, and infinitely worthy of love. But I think there is some sense in which all sentient beings and all beings that can rationally pursue their own vision of the Good are fascinating, valuable, and worthy of love. I wrote in a review of Martha Nussbaum’s Justice for Animals:

Nussbaum highlights three essential virtues in thinking about animals: wonder, which draws our attention to the value of animals; compassion, which alerts us to suffering; and outrage without the desire for retribution, which motivates us to improve the world. Compassion and outrage are common and valued in the animal advocacy community, but wonder is rarer.

The virtue of wonder is both amazement at animals’ unique ways of life and curiosity about why they behave the way they do. When we wonder at an animal, we recognize that their behavior has a purpose, that there is something it is like to be them, and we try to understand. Wonder, she writes, “takes us out of ourselves and toward the other… [It has] nothing to do with our own personal search for well-being. It is connected to our original joy at life itself.”

All sentient beings are a proper object of compassion and wonder, simply by virtue of being sentient. We can only feel a certain amount of wonder at a time; if I feel wonder at a dolphin’s echolocation, then I’m not feeling it about the problem-solving abilities of octopuses. But that doesn’t make the octopuses any less deserving of wonder. And if I am awestruck by octopuses, who can’t even comprehend the concept of taking the Giving What We Can pledge, then perhaps I can also feel awe at myself, in spite of my difficulties budgeting to fulfill same.

But the second part of the quote—affirming weakness as a way to aim high—is something I desperately feel the need for, and something I don’t have a good answer to.

I don’t have God’s grace to rely on to make the gap between my ideals and my shortcomings bearable. Like the authors of All The Lives You Can Change, I observe that most people in the secular world dial down their standards until they’re achievable, and I refuse to do so; I am not going to settle for being a decent person. But I don’t believe in God. I don’t even believe I can become God. And I don’t have a great answer for how to deal with my inevitable failures and shortcomings without being able to rely on the grace of a being I don’t think exists. But I do think it’s worth taking seriously as an aspect of how to live well in a world beyond the reach of God.

1

Implicitly Protestant—not a ton of references to the Pope or the Church Fathers here.

2

I am a weird kind of Protestant and only dubiously a Christian at all. The atheism is a bit of a problem.

3

Although I’m discussing AI here, a similar argument applies to nuclear war and bioengineered pandemics.

4

Or a substantial fraction of the value in the universe, if AIs are sentient.

5

This is the Quaker eschatology, so I’m fond of it.

6

And then he remarks that the solution to this problem is to “hurry up and become God.”

7

So far, growth mindset.

item.title: Donation recommendations for effective altruists (July 2026)
item.description: My recommendation for donors who are American citizens or permanent residents is that they donate directly to high-value political candidates.
item.content:encoded:
My recommendation for donors who are American citizens or permanent residents is that they donate directly to high-value political candidates.1

My recommendation for other donors is the GiveWell All Grants Fund, except other donors with idiosyncratic preferences who should donate to other things.

Why Is Donald Trump Bad?

U. S. Democracy

Let’s be clear about this: the current president of the United States tried to do a coup to overthrow the results of a free and fair election which he lost.

It’s true it was an ineffectual coup that had little chance of succeeding. Once upon a time, however, attempting any coup would have ruled out someone from the presidency, and “well, he wasn’t very good at it” wasn’t considered a defense.

Donald Trump’s first presidency was remarkably similar to a normal Republican presidency. The norms and institutions of American democracy managed to check his most autocratic impulses. His aides managed to work around him to get governing done. You wouldn’t have been unreasonable, in December 2024, to predict that Trump’s second term would mostly just be embarrassing.

Unfortunately, Trump has learned from his mistakes. At present, Trump is actively pursuing the consolidation of power in the executive branch. It’s easy to get caught up in the endless waves of bad news from the Trump administration, many of which doesn’t distinguish the important (ICE mobilizations) from the goofy (the Reflecting Pool continues greenish) to the frankly gossipy (Olivia Nuzzi said what in her memoir?). But let me try to lay out the situation as clearly as I can.

Trump has used retaliatory arrests and prosecutions against his political opponents—something he’d explicitly promised to do before being elected. He is openly rewarding people and corporations for donations with high-level government positions, pardons, and political favors. Trump has profited from the presidency to the tune of $3 billion, including bribes from authoritarian dictatorships like Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates.2

Trump is taking control of traditionally independent positions in the civil service—from prosecutors to the head of the Bureau of Labor Statistics to the National Science Board—and trying to fill them with political loyalists who will do his bidding. The Supreme Court’s recent Trump v. Slaughter decision found that the president has the power to remove independent agency heads (other than the Fed) at will, further increasing Trump’s power.

Trump is is subverting the checks and balances placed upon his power by the Constitution. He has openly defied as many as one in three court orders against him. He has broken the law to avoid spending money allocated by Congress. He has taken power from the states—most famously by deploying California’s National Guard without the consent of the governor of California. He has also targeted the institutions of civil society that are supposed to check the power of the president: the press, law firms, universities. The administration has publicly stated that any leftists who protest that the government is violating their rights are lying. His disrespect for the Constitution extends to trying to end birthright citizenship, one of the most fundamental rights protected by the Fourteenth Amendment.

Most frighteningly, Trump has continued to say he won the 2020 election. He pardoned the January 6 rioters who, again, tried to perform a coup against the U.S. government to make him president. He tried (and fortunately failed) to create a $1.8 billion fund to pay off victims of “weaponization and lawfare”, i.e. people prosecuted for election tampering or attempted insurrection. He has targeted the people who prosecuted the January 6 rioters. He is meddling with the 2030 Census, which will govern apportionment and the Electoral College for the next decade. He has hinted publicly at wanting to run for an unconstitutional third term. Trump continues to use false claims about election integrity to claim unconstitutional federal authority over elections.

I find the behavior of Secretary of War Pete Hegseth particularly worrying. A friend of mine who works in U.S. defense policy says:

So, if I was Hegseth, and trying to plot a coup, my main plan would be “fire people until the military coughs up someone more loyal to Trump than the Constitution”, which would take a while, but I might block promotions of the politically suspect (women and African-Americans), fire existing popular leadership so there wasn’t an obvious person to coalesce around as resistance, and try to increase morale and popularity with a bunch of dumb ideas. Getting us into a war would probably help on the margin.

To be clear, Hegseth might not be trying to stage a coup! He might just be doing a horrifically bad job as Secretary of War. But if he was trying to prepare to stage a coup, it’s not obvious what he would be doing differently.

Metaculus forecasts a relatively high level of threat to U.S. democracy; however, I find the Threat Index a bit hard to interpret. It also forecasts a 15% chance that the U.S. is no longer a democracy by 2030 but that one has fewer predictions.

Now, the situation is not quite as dire as it is in other countries backsliding from democracy. Trump has to prioritize removing independent civil servants because the U.S. government has a strong norm of an independent civil service and apolitical military; many other autocrats came to office with a civil service that was already seen as a tool of the presidency’s will and a source of patronage for its clients. Trump has defied the courts, but he hasn’t been able to fully bring them under his control. And Trump has mostly stuck to removing federal funding from civil-society institutions; he has yet to do mass arrests of his political enemies or make significant use of state-supported political violence.

But the Trump administration’s subversion of democratic norms is shockingly rapid. And instead of slowly going institution by institution, the Trump administration has attacked democratic norms on all levels simultaneously.

I also think U.S. democracy is far more important than democracy in Brazil or Turkey—at least for people who don’t live in any of those countries. On a practical level, America is currently the global hegemon. America being authoritarian, hostile to other countries, and irrational affects every country in the world. As one example, freedom of navigation—the principle that ships should be free to move in international waters—is enforced by the U.S. Navy. If the US does not back freedom of the seas, global shipping becomes wildly more expensive at best and impossible at worst. In that case, many places that aren’t America would face economic collapse and starvation. That is merely one example of what can go wrong if America becomes a dictatorship run by a corrupt, irresponsible, incompetent man who is actively opposed to America’s role in the international order.

On a symbolic level, America is the best-known country in the world and a beacon of capitalist, liberal democracy, the best system of government ever invented. If we fall to illiberal autocracy, it emboldens dictators and human-rights violators all around the world. The sense that human rights, liberalism, and democracy are good things is a very real constraint on what abusive governments can do. America’s human rights track record—at home and abroad—is hardly spotless. But it sure as hell beats China or Russia. And I don’t think we’re going to like what happens when we replace an international order where governments give lip service to human rights with one of unrestrained will to power.

USAID

Under the Trump administration, USAID has been de facto destroyed. Fortunately, we’re not in the absolute worst-case scenario many people worried about in early 2025. Much of the funding has been restored, although not to previous levels. Foreign aid is now under the aegis of the State Department, which has a lot of other stuff going on and doesn’t have the institutional knowledge that USAID had. (This is a good article about the current state of U.S. foreign aid and this is a good article about the current state of PEPFAR.)

USAID was very far from a perfect organization. Indeed, much of the money spent by USAID was spent in ways that underperformed just giving people the cash, and much of the organization was resistant to adopting more evidence-based policies. But, ultimately, U.S. foreign aid saved 3.3 million lives per year. Because the Trump administration callously smashed the foreign-aid infrastructure without any thought for how to replace it, millions of people are going to die. But, sure, we saved the Africans from woke DEI operas.

Can we expect a Democrat to increase funding to foreign aid and organize it in some more sensible way? Probably, yes. USAID spent sixty years as an uncontroversial bipartisan program. USAID was cut, not out of principled Republican opposition to foreign aid, but because of the idiosyncratic personal views of Elon Musk. Foreign aid, although unpopular, is a low-salience issue where the views of politicians and policymakers dominate. Politicians and policymakers like saving lives, particularly when it costs them nothing to do so.

The Iran War

I cannot believe I have to put a new section in this post.

The war with Iran has been an unmitigated humanitarian and foreign-policy disaster. It has weakened the United States’s international reputation and emboldened Iran, which now believes that it can stand up to a full-on military assault by the United States. It has accomplished nothing to bring freedom to the Iranian people. The blockage of the Strait of Hormuz has raised oil and fertilizer prices worldwide. That means that millions of people will go without food and the supply chains for crucial medicines and vaccines will be disrupted. And, as always during wars, many innocent people are going to die.

I still remember when people said that we should vote for Trump because he wouldn’t entrap us in foreign-policy adventurism.

Artificial Intelligence?

The common-sense case for AI regulation is very simple. If the CEOs of the companies developing a technology go around, in public, saying that they think that a technology might drive humanity extinct, our regulatory approach shouldn’t be #yolo.

You don’t have to go full Eliezer Yudkowsky to support AI regulation. The vast majority of technologies-- new cancer treatments, better solar panels, balance bikes-- have a 0% chance of causing human extinction. If something has a 0.1% chance of causing human extinction, that entirely justifies staffing a division of regulators to ask pointed questions of the manufacturers.

I was convinced by this article that the date at which we will achieve artificial general intelligence is bimodal: either it will happen by 2030-2032, or it will be several decades away.3 The author of this article puts about 50/50 odds on each possibility. I’m not sure I’d go that far, but even a 5% chance of the development of AGI by 2030 is frightening.

If we get AGI soon, the Trump administration will develop the executive-branch regulations that govern this technology. It will also play a leadership role in getting laws passed about AGI. I find this worrying for several reasons. First, across policy areas, the Trump administration has shown little interest in consulting with experts or implementing evidence-based policies; it has eviscerated technocratic institutions and replaced them with political spoils for Trump loyalists. Do you want the man who appointed Robert F. Kennedy Jr. as Health Secretary or Pete Hegseth as Secretary of War to make decisions about a very important, very complex emerging technology? I don’t.

Second, Trump is specifically getting advice from Marc Andreessen. You can read Marc Andreessen’s views on AI here. It is rather short on arguments that we shouldn’t be worried about AI risk, and long on accusations of AI safety advocates being a conspiracy theorist cult who read too much Mary Shelley. Nothing to worry about here! Surely if there’s one thing we’ve learned in the past twenty years it’s to trust in the disinterested, self-sacrificial altruism of tech billionaires.

Much like a fossil-fuel executive advising about climate policy, or a tobacco company executive advising about the harms of smoking, Marc Andreessen has no interest in admitting any harms or risks of his technology that might reduce his profit margins. This is a completely reckless approach to regulation of any powerful new technology.

Why Donations?

How Do Donations Help?

No one really knows how much it costs to flip a vote, sorry. Political moneyball is insanely complicated. Money can be spent well or wasted. No amount of money can convince voters to vote for an unelectable candidate; on the other hand, good candidate selection can make money go much farther. In some cases, it’s even possible for additional money to make a candidate less likely to get elected.4

But it does seem obviously true that at least some ways of spending money make candidates more likely to win elections. Voter registration and get-out-the-vote efforts probably remind some people that elections are happening and convince them that they want to vote rather than scroll TikTok. If people have heard of a candidate and have some idea what she stands for, they might vote for her. Ozy’s Mom (my normie liberal focus group) often votes for local or statewide offices where she hasn’t heard of any of the candidates, so she picks either the woman or the person with an Asian-sounding or Latino-sounding surname. Advertisements can improve on this ignoble status quo.

Politicians spend a lot of time fundraising: some estimates suggest Congresspeople spend as much as 50% of their time fundraising. You have heard that calling your Congressperson is a good way to make your opinions known. But your voice goes farther if you donate.

Why To Candidates?

You should make donations directly to candidates (”hard money” donations).

Money given directly to a candidate goes farther because:

  • Candidates get better rates on advertisements than non-candidates.

  • Outside groups aren’t allowed to coordinate with candidates. Hard-money donations allow candidates to have a unified strategy based on what does best in their internal polling. Money is less likely to be wasted through duplicating effort some other group has already made.

  • Candidates, even in safe seats, are expected to fundraise “dues” for their party to help their party win more contested elections. Candidates who want powerful positions like committee chairs are expected to raise even more. These dues come from their hard-money funds. So donating to your candidate gives them more influence.

A friend of mine says that campaign finance legislation is set up to give the top 10% more influence at the expense of the top 1%. How does this work?

The most you can donate to a federal political candidate is $7000 ($3,500 for the primary and $3,500 for the general). In many states, state-level candidates also have limits.

In conventional nonprofits, most funding comes from a small number of very rich people. For example, more than half of effective altruist funding comes from Coefficient Giving, which is mostly funded by a single person, Dustin Moskovitz.

If you maxed out donations to all the candidates I presently recommend, you would donate $64,000. That’s a pretty big chunk of change, but it’s approximately the donation budget of an American with 99th percentile income who has taken the Giving What We Can pledge. That is also exactly the same amount as Dustin Moskovitz can donate to my recommended candidates.5

In short, hard-money donations to political candidates are a very important area where the low-hanging fruit cannot possibly be picked by billionaires.

Who Shouldn’t Donate?

In the United States, your direct political donations to candidates are publicly available information. This doesn’t matter for most people; it might matter for you.

The most important caveat:

If you are willing and able to take a political appointee position in the Trump administration, you shouldn’t make a donation to Democrats or anti-Trump Republicans (e.g. Rep. Thomas Massie) and you should probably take the position.

If you are willing and able to take a civil service position in the Trump administration, you should think carefully before making a donation and you should probably take the position.6

Obviously, you shouldn’t take a position that makes the Trump administration more effective at overthrowing American democracy. But the first Trump administration was an ordinary Republican administration because a huge number of policymakers, advisors, and civil servants thwarted Trump’s authoritarian instincts. To the extent you can put yourself in a position to do the same, you should.

Many heroic people serve in the Trump administration as political appointees: keeping vaccines somewhat more accessible, making AI regulation somewhat saner, preserving whatever scraps of foreign aid they can, being one more voice in the the Department of War or the State Department or the Department of Justice who will stand in the face of authoritarianism and say “no.” Consider how principled and conflict-friendly you are, get support from people who will hold you to your moral standards, save your money so you can quit if necessary, and take the job.

The vast majority of jobs in the US government are Civil Service roles. It is illegal for the government to discriminate in hiring for civil service roles based on your political affiliation, including your donations. However, the Trump administration has been known to break laws, and anecdotal evidence suggests that civil servants have faced career consequences for their political donations. Think carefully before donating.

You may not be well-suited to taking a job in the Trump administration. However, if you want certain political appointee positions, a history of donations to Democrats may hurt you. Here is a helpful quiz to help you figure out if you should avoid donating.

Most donation forms say that you can’t donate if you’re a federal contractor. This is primarily a restriction on sole proprietors and corporations. If you happen to work for a company that contracts with the federal government, you’re still allowed to donate.

Where To Donate?

Thing of Things recommends donating to Manny Rutinel, who is running in Colorado’s 8th District. Rutinel is a strong advocate for farmed animal welfare and for sensible regulation of AI (e.g. he supported whistleblower protections for AI lab employees).

People who prioritize AI safety should also donate to Scott Wiener, who is running in California’s 11th district. Scott Wiener’s campaigning led to SB-53, which requires companies to have some plan to prevent catastrophic AI-related outcomes. Because of California’s top-two primary system, Wiener is running against another Democrat. So non-AI-safety-focused donors shouldn’t donate to Wiener, because a Democrat will definitely represent San Francisco no matter what. On the other hand, Wiener’s campaign is a particularly good use of money for AI-safety-focused donors, because it’s much cheaper to convince Democrats to support a particular Democrat than to convince Republicans to support a Democrat.

If you are a Republican who is concerned about AI safety, consider reaching out to the AI Policy Network, who will be happy to recommend Republican donation targets.

If you have more money burning a hole in your donations budget, Thing of Things follows Slow Boring’s recommendations.

To flip the House and Senate:

  • Bobby Pulido (U.S. House, TX-15)

  • Josh Turek (U.S. Senate, Iowa)

  • Mary Peltola (Alaska)

  • Bill Hill (Alaska at-large)

  • Johnny Garcia (TX-35)

  • Don Davis (NC-01)

  • Lindsay James (IA-2)

  • Bale Dalton (FL-7)

Some state-level races are important for redistricting. This is a more morally complicated situation. I am opposed to gerrymandering, even if it benefits Democrats. But as long as Republicans have an advantage from their own gerrymandering, Democrats won’t achieve fairness by refusing to gerrymander themselves. Nevertheless, I think it makes sense to refuse to donate to advance gerrymandeirng.

For redistricting:

  • Anita Earls (North Carolina Supreme Court)

  • Keisha Lance Bottoms (Georgia governor)

  • Eileen Hartnett Albillar (Pennsylvania’s Sixth Senate District)

  • Sara Agerton (Pennsylvania House District 88)

  • John Kroll (Wisconsin’s Assembly District 85)

If you don’t want to subscribe to Slow Boring, I will rerun this post when Matt Yglesias comes out with new recommendations.

Lobbying Congresspeople You Donate To

Some candidates’ donation portals will allow you to include a message. You can always call a candidate’s offices and say that you maxed out your donations because you care about $issue, which I understand candidates do take into account. You will probably not get to talk to a candidate unless you’re e.g. a bundler who convinces a number of individuals to donate.

Donations for Non-Americans, the Apolitical, Future Republican Staffers, Et Cetera

Most donors should give to the GiveWell All Grants Fund. The USAID cuts mean that global poverty donations go farther than ever before. The GiveWell All Grants Fund allows GiveWell to use its own discretion to make grants, which means that it has more flexibility to respond to the confusing and ever-changing aid cuts situation. GiveWell chose their Top Charities in a very different aid environment, in which U.S. foreign aid had some priority areas—such as HIV and health-systems strengthening7—well-handled. Donating to the All Grants Fund allows GiveWell to make time-sensitive grants in these areas, even though GiveWell has yet to complete full Top Charities investigations.

Donors with particular idiosyncratic beliefs may want to give to other global poverty charities. Specifically:

  • Because malaria causes miscarriages, donating to the Against Malaria Foundation is by far the most effective charity for pro-life donors.

  • GiveWell is exploring programs such as giving farmed animals to developing-world farmers. Certain animal advocates may prefer to give to the GiveWell Top Charities Fund so that none of their money goes to purchasing farmed animals.

Donors who value animals at a significant fraction of the amount they value humans may continue to want to donate to animal advocacy. Some donors may also want to donate to animal advocacy for other reasons (for example, to offset meat consumption).

  • Donors who plan to donate over $10,000 a year and who care about farmed insects, farmed shrimps, or wild animals should contact Rethink Priorities to participate in their Neglected Animals Program, which collects publicly unavailable information to help medium-sized donors make the best decisions about helping neglected animals.

  • Donors who prefer a high level of certainty should donate to the Navigation Fund’s cage-free egg campaign fund. Cage-free egg campaigns affect chickens (who are almost certainly sentient) and are among the only animal advocacy interventions that have been conclusively shown to work.

  • Other donors should donate to the EA Animal Welfare Fund. You can find the most recent information about their plans here and their most recent payout report here.

Some donors may continue to prioritize global priorities research. In this case, I continue to endorse Rethink Priorities as the most exciting organization working in the space. Rethink Priorities’s research addresses some of the most important issues of our time, from farmed salmon welfare to ending lead poisoning to digital minds. Their approach is empirical: instead of ungrounded philosophical speculation, they dig deep into the evidence and find insights that people can actually use. They do consulting for real nonprofits, which keeps them connected to what nonprofits actually need. I am reliably impressed by Rethink Priorities’ reports and always learn something when I read them.

Thanks to Keller Scholl, Eric Neyman, and three anonymous people. All mistakes are my own.

3

Of course, AI timelines are controversial among people who are worried about AI.

4

Effective altruists may remember the case of Carrick Flynn, where excessive soft money from FTX’s SuperPAC may have made voters see him as an out-of-touch “crypto candidate” being forced on them by Sam Bankman-Fried.

He can, of course, max out his donations to all Democratic political candidates, but even then any individual Democratic candidate will have trouble winning an election with nothing but $7000 of Moskbuxx.

If you are potentially interested in working in the Trump administration and are interested in emerging technologies (artificial intelligence or bioengineering), you can go here for advising.

item.title: You can't join the secret inner circle of cool effective altruists
item.description: I, and a lot of other people I know, seem to believe something like this:
item.content:encoded:
I, and a lot of other people I know, seem to believe something like this:1

Somewhere out there, there are the cool, high-impact effective altruists who are really having a positive effect on the world. They are all invited to lots of awesome parties with other cool, high-impact effective altruists. They have rich networks of supportive friends and polycules full of attractive, sexually free people of their preferred genders. They know all kinds of secrets that us normal people don’t know, and they laugh at us for our out-of-touch takes. They can get jobs and grants by having a fifteen-minute conversation with a friend or a friend of a friend. They don’t have to slog through endless and dispiriting job applications, throwing out a hundred apps to get nothing back but “we had a very strong pool this time.” They never sit at home alone on weekends scrolling TikTok and contemplating doing their laundry. They can go to all the coolest co-working spaces AND EA Global.

This viewpoint is (a) not true (b) unhelpful for achieving any reasonable goal.

In this post, I’m going to be talking mostly about effective altruism, but I suspect similar dynamics are also true of other networking-heavy communities with some people who are extremely successful and some people who can’t figure out how to break in (academia, writing, acting, non-effective-altruist nonprofit work).

That Is Not How Anything Works

I am, arguably, part of the secret circle of cool effective altruists. I have friends who work for Anthropic and Lightcone Infrastructure. I am at least friendly acquaintances with many writers you’ve heard of (Kelsey Piper, Scott Alexander, Eliezer Yudkowsky). Every article about the Bay Area effective altruism community is contractually obligated to include my friends’ group house and their habit of singing Landsailor before Friday night Shabbat.

You know who all these statements are also true of? My coparent Lindsey, who dropped out of college because he couldn’t hack it, works as an elementary-school teacher, and was my first choice to give the speech at my Solstice about being a failed effective altruist.2

And he didn’t get those connections through me—in fact, he’s closer to many Official Cool Effective Altruists than I am.

The reason is that no emotionally healthy person picks their friends by ranking everyone they know from highest impact to lowest impact and then proceeding steadily down the list until they’re out of social spoons. People choose their friends based on proximity, common interests, shared values, idiosyncratic personal chemistry, how convenient they are for scheduling D&D, etc. Most social groups with a lot of Official Cool Effective Altruists also have a lot of normal people, or even people who are quite low-status.

Furthermore, there isn’t one Secret Inner Circle of Cool Effective Altruists. There are many different inner circles, many of which don’t like each other very much. The leadership of Pause AI isn’t exactly going to Anthropic house parties, and neither has a ton of overlap with GiveWell leadership or the Secret Masters of Animal Advocacy.

It’s reasonable to want to be friends with Official Cool Effective Altruists-- they’re usually strikingly kind and interesting people, they probably want to talk about AI or cause prioritization as much as you do, it can be good networking (but see section three). But I think a lot of people want to be friends with the Official Cool Effective Altruists as a form of validation-- this proves that you’re successful and intelligent and high-impact and really able to make the world better. Unfortunately, whom you’re friends with provides almost zero information about whether you’re successful and intelligent and high-impact.

A lot of people (i.e. me) assume that, if you never see someone at parties, it’s because the person is going to secret even cooler parties that you aren’t invited to. In reality, in my experience, Official Cool Effective Altruists are sometimes attending cool parties I’m not invited to, but very often are instead:

1. Working.3
2. Playing Starcraft in their underwear while listening to bad metal and binging on vegan beef jerky.

Try not to believe in the Cool Parties of the Gaps.

We Would Not Want It To Be How Anything Works

I think people normally get invested in befriending The Secret Inner Circle of Cool Effective Altruists because they want something else: supportive friends and a healthy community, or a job in effective altruism, or even just being able to text their favorite blogger and get a response. All of those are reasonable things to want. But, thank goodness, befriending The Secret Inner Circle of Cool Effective Altruists is a terrible way to achieve those goals. We’re not that far gone!

Are there people who only want to be friends with high-impact people? Yes, of course. But they are a minority of effective altruists with impressive achievements, and whatever their merits as grantmakers or global priorities researchers, they suck and you deserve better than being friends with them.

Why? Because people who only want to be friends with high-impact people quietly drop their friends for being low-impact. So if you lose your job, or go through a mental health crisis, or get diagnosed with a chronic illness, suddenly you find your so-called friends aren’t returning your DMs—at exactly the time you need your friends the most.

Befriending these people isn’t even the best thing for doing good in the world! A lot of the best career paths are risky, and you’re going to be able to take more risks if you know that, if you fail, your friends will be there for you.

It’s important not to mix up “job that improves the world” with “job that makes people I admire think I’m cool.” Effective altruists fall victim to groupthink just like anyone else. Very likely, the effective altruism community is making serious errors. It’s possible that the most valuable path to impact (in general or for you specifically) is someone no one thinks of as an “effective altruist career.” But if your friends chose you based on your impact, you’re not going to be looking for the truth about these questions, you’re going to be looking for the answer that makes your friends respect you. As Upton Sinclair would have said if he’d thought of it, it is difficult to get a man to understand something, when his access to fun parties with hot tubs depends upon his not understanding it.

Now, getting hired in effective altruism is hard. Networking matters in effective altruism as it does in any other field. Some effective altruist jobs are only available to people who have a good reputation in the effective altruist community, for reasons I wrote about in this post. You can’t tell from a resume if someone is a kind, reliable person with good judgment, so people tend to hire for many sensitive positions from within their networks.

However, in every effective altruist workplace I have ever interacted with, hiring is based on the hiring manager’s best assessment of whether you can do the work. People with only tangential involvement in the effective altruist community are regularly hired over heavily involved effective altruists, because they are better at the job. Indeed, in my experience, effective altruist hiring is far more likely to involve blinded work trials than non-effective-altruist hiring is—in part to prevent the bias of people hiring their friends and acquaintances. And once you’re senior enough that people are hiring for good judgment, having former coworkers and bosses who think well of you is way more important than whatever you do in your off time.

Also. Let me be blunt here. If you get an effective altruist job over a more skilled alternative candidate because you’re friends with the right people, then your effective altruist work is actually worse for the world than you not doing anything. You would literally have made the world better off if you had spent your time getting in stupid fights on Reddit about fake Am I The Asshole? stories.

If you want, you can think of not attending parties as heroically saving the effective altruist community from poor talent allocation.

There Are Better Ways To Achieve Your Goals

I have occasionally amused myself at events by watching people try to suck up to Scott Alexander.4 If you want Scott Alexander—or any other effective altruist microcelebrity—to think well of you, you need to treat them like a normal person. If you instead act like a supplicant begging for any bits of wisdom that drop from their lips, or vomit up your entire curriculum vitae to show that you’re worthy to participate in this conversation, or pick stupid fights to show that you’re not overawed by them, they will be uncomfortable and not want to spend more time with you than etiquette demands.

In general, the more you try to impress people, the weirder you act, and the less impressed they are by you. You are far more likely to actually impress people if you’re fine with the possibility that they’ll think you’re stupid, annoying, boring, or a jerk. Being really invested in joining the Secret Inner Circle of Cool Effective Altruists makes you worse at befriending people you admire.

Doing effective altruist work has a far lower barrier to entry than getting an effective altruist job. If you want a job in communications or technical AI safety research or global priorities research or investigative journalism, you can literally just do that shit on your own, write up your results, and post it somewhere people will read. Hiring managers at effective-altruism-associated nonprofits really do follow LessWrong and the Effective Altruism Forum, and if your work there is impressive you are far more likely to get a job.

Some jobs—like fundraising, accounting, or ops jobs—are difficult to impossible to do without an employer. In those cases, the best course of action is often to get a job doing the same kind of work for a less competitive, non-effective-altruism-associated employer, and then switch into effective altruist work once you’ve built enough skills that they won’t have to train you on the job.5

Now, you might be thinking “I wouldn’t know where to begin doing investigative journalism on my own” or “I have been posting my global priorities research but no one reads it” or “I can’t get hired doing ops for anyone, even for-profit businesses.” In that case, your problem is that you don’t have the skills you need to do the job, and should (a) git gud or (b) give up. Either of those options is better than pursuing the Secret Inner Circle of Cool Effective Altruists, which will get you party invitations and not job offers because you still won’t be very good at your job.

Finally, if you want a healthy supportive community, don’t strategize about how to appeal to the highest-status effective altruists you can. Instead, strategize about how you can meet people whom you like, who share your values, and who make you a better person when you’re around them—regardless of whether their impact is legible or even extant. To be sure, finding a community like that is also very hard. But it’s much easier to achieve your goal if you’re actually pursuing the right one in the first place.

If you already have a healthy supportive community, be grateful for what you have. Don’t neglect the best things in your life in a futile quest for the approval of imaginary cool people.

You Will Never Join The Secret Inner Circle of Cool Effective Altruists

Like I said, I am arguably part of the secret inner circle of cool effective altruists. And yet I also have this anxiety. I have friends who are even more incontrovertibly in the secret inner circle of cool effective altruists than I am, and many of them still have this anxiety.

The reason is that there is always a more inner circle. To someone who doesn’t live in the Bay Area, I’m part of the Secret Inner Circle of Cool Effective Altruists. From my perspective, I’m on the outside, and the real Secret Inner Circle is Anthropic employees or people who work at the Constellation coworking space. If I worked at Anthropic or at Constellation, I’d think I was on the outside, and the real Secret Inner Circle were the people who sit at the cool kids’ table at lunch. If I sat at the cool kids’ table at lunch, I’d think I was on the outside, and the real Secret Inner Circle are the people who are part of Dario Amodei’s group chat, Lightcone Takeover & Optimization Planning (Let’s Make A Dyson Sphere Out Of Mercury). And if I were part of Lightcone Takeover & Optimization Planning, I’d think I was on the outside, and the real Secret Inner Circle is the second group chat Amanda Askell made to shittalk people she doesn’t like in the first group chat.

And remember what I said about how there are a number of inner circles which often don’t like each other much? Even if you are in Amanda Askell’s secret shittalking group chat, you almost certainly aren’t also in, I don’t know, the group chat where Ray Arnold figures out who’s going to be creative lead for the next Bay Area Winter Solstice. You can be sitting there, reading Amanda Askell’s snark about other people’s bad plans for Mercury, going “I am being excluded from the chat the real cool kids are in, where they argue for three hundred hours about what version of Somebody Will we’re going to do this year.”

“The cool insiders who know what’s really going on and who are invited to all the best parties” is one of those irregularly declining nouns. That guy over there is a cool insider who knows what’s really going on and who is invited to all the best parties. You are a successful networker with a thriving social life. I just have friends.

That’s because “the cool insiders who know what’s really going on and who are invited to all the best parties” are like 5% an actual group6 and 95% a projection of your insecurities. As soon as you actually get to know someone cool, they start having their own traits which have nothing to do with what makes you feel worst about yourself. So you feel accepted for like two weeks, and then you start projecting on some other group you’re not part of, because the problem was never social acceptance in the first place.

You will never be able to get validation and acceptance from the anthropomorphic personification of all your deepest insecurities, because we haven’t got any of those in the effective altruist community. All we have is Alice, who keeps losing her house keys, feels insecure about whether her research direction will pay off, often skips parties to play Starcraft in her underwear while listening to bad metal and binging on vegan beef jerky, and is the first author on half a dozen important papers in technical AI safety.

You might be able to be friends with Alice. You will never be able to be friends with the Secret Inner Circle of Cool Effective Altruists. I generally advise having desires it is in theory possible to achieve.

1

If this post seems familiar, it’s because it’s a new version of an older post; I didn’t like how the older one came out and I wanted to do another take on it.

2

Me: but if I suggest anyone else gives a speech about being a failed effective altruist, they’ll get mad at me!

Lindsey: ...

3

Many Official Cool Effective Altruists seem to believe that work-life balance is a scam invented by Big Deontology to sell more low-impact charity.

4

I am sometimes an unvirtuous person.

5

I don’t mean here to neglect the important role that luck plays in whether you get a high-impact job. Many talented people don’t get a high-impact job because Lady Luck hasn’t smiled on them. This is also true if you attend all the right parties.

6

Dario Amodei presumably does have a groupchat and you presumably do get to learn some interesting stuff if you’re in it.

item.content:encoded:
I stole the title and thesis of this post from the great etirabys and arguably I should just link her post. But I have been linking people her post for FIVE FUCKING YEARS and the dating market inefficiency under discussion still exists. So I have decided to write my own contribution to the discourse in the hope that it will finally cause straight women to act in their enlightened self-interest.

Consider, if you will, all the traits you want in a man that other women also want. Funny. Emotionally mature. Willing to do his fair share of the chores. Handsome. Buff. Rich. Tall. Fantastic at sex. Kind. Intelligent. Interesting. Ambitious. Good at music or dancing. Famous????? Wants children. Doesn’t want children. Willing to commit. Hopelessly devoted to you, eager to please, and willing to walk five hundred miles and walk five hundred more just to be the man who walked a thousand miles to fall down at your door.

It is possible to get a man with far more of those traits than you would normally be able to get with your flat ass, spotty employment history, stressful emotional problems, and indifference to wearing makeup.

This is because a large population of objectively attractive men simply won’t put any concerted effort into getting dates. Some of these men are chronically loveshy and have very little romantic experience; others have dated in the past, but are currently going through a sexually unsuccessful period. Many objectively attractive men are single for no other reason than that they won’t hit on women, and you can date well out of your league if you ask them out.

(I would advise that men who have trouble dating consider whether to read this post-- I am going to be blunt and somewhat objectifying about men who have trouble dating, and I don’t want to make you guys feel bad.)

Why This Happens

What? How does this happen? That sounds fake.

In my experience (both personally and when I was a life coach), men don’t put any effort into dating for several different reasons.

Some men are simply too busy to actively date. They have an active social life, a demanding job, or enriching and absorbing hobbies. They’d make time for a real girlfriend, but they don’t feel like they have time to waste sending insipid messages on Bumble.

Some men dislike dating apps. At present, dating occurs overwhelmingly on The Apps. Dating apps tend to emphasize pictures, leaving viewers with only a few sentences of text to get to know the person behind the profile. Dating apps are a particularly bad fit for men who don’t care much about physical appearance and who are primarily attracted to women based on their personalities. I have known many men to object to my advice that they should use The Apps because they literally don’t know how to tell if a woman is attractive from a picture (and at least one man to claim he needs to first read 10,000 words of her blog posts).

Relatedly, some men do poorly on dating apps. This is the flip side of the previous problem. Dating apps reward tall men with attractive faces who photograph well. But most women tend to weight other traits more highly—charisma, sense of humor, talents, intelligence, kindness. Most women wouldn’t actually reject a charming, funny man who happens to be 5’10”. But these men can have a frustrating time on the dating apps—sending out messages that no one ever responds to, spending hours swiping without a date to show for it—and often wind up quitting.

Some men have never really had the opportunity to date. They may have been focusing on their careers or studies. They may have grown up in a conservative religious group and deconverted. They may have had success-focused (stereotypically, immigrant) parents who strongly discouraged dating and socializing. They may have had male-dominated hobbies and a male-dominated friend group that left them with no opportunity to meet women. They might have undergone some personal tragedy, such as the death of a loved one or a chronic illness. It is often possible to snap up these men before they enter the dating pool.

Some men never learned how to date. They’re mystified by how to flirt, tell if a woman is interested in them, ask women out, plan a date, or figure out when to kiss her. Because the process of dating seems mysterious and incomprehensible—not to mention full of landmines where you accidentally sexually harass someone—they avoid dating.

Some men experience internalized desexualization—the belief that your sexual and romantic desires are cringe, pathetic, and burdensome on others, and it is delusional to expect to fulfill them. Naturally, these men don’t put any effort into dating. Why would you waste time on dating if no one would ever be attracted to you? Surely the selfless approach is to hide forever his deepest, darkest, most shameful secret—that he would really like to hold a woman’s hand.

Of course, many men avoid dating for multiple reasons. If a man is already quite busy, then he’s unlikely to want to message women on The Apps at random in the hope that one of them turns out to have an intriguing personality. Men who never had the opportunity to date often don’t learn how to date, so once they have a chance they don’t know what to do. Lack of success on dating apps can feed into internalized desexualization. Etc.

These problems aren’t more common among men than among women. But pretty women are much more likely than men to be asked out, even if they put zero effort into dating. They might have fewer choices than if they put any effort into dating, but there is a reasonable chance that they’ll manage to date someone.

But because straight women don’t ask men out, a man who doesn’t put any effort into dating simply won’t get any dates—even if he is otherwise a desirable boyfriend or husband. (Women who aren’t pretty and don’t put any effort into dating are in a similar position to men here.)

Are you saying that these men are so niiiiiiiiiiice I should give them a chaaaaaaaance?

Absolutely not.

I feel bad for kind but generally unattractive men, but I’m not going to write a whole long post trying to convince you to date them; that’s not good for you or them. What drove me to write is the number of chronically single men I’ve run into who are objectively really good romantic partners—cute, fun to be around, smart, interesting, kind, generous, emotionally mature, and prepared to endlessly dote on their hypothetical girlfriend that they don’t have. “Kind but unattractive people can’t get dates” is sad, but an inevitable feature of human mating preferences. “Kind, interesting, handsome, funny, emotionally mature people can’t get dates” is PERVERSE. I refuse to believe that we can’t do better.

I believe the correct approach to asking men out is a little healthy self-indulgence, like opening a box of chocolates and considering whether you’re more in the mood for almond or coconut today. Ask out the hottest guy in the room! Ask out the guy with the most adventurous life! Ask out the guy you start talking to and then suddenly it’s six hours later and you’ve been ignoring everyone else at the party and they’re all annoyed with you! Ask out your favorite Internet microcelebrity!

Don’t ask a man out unless you’re actively excited about the prospect of going on a date with him. (Not necessarily about getting married to him and having six babies, but about the prospect of spending an evening in his company.) This is a matter of time management. Once you’ve unlocked the secret of asking men out, if you have low standards, you could easily have four dates a week and no time to knit while listening to romantasy audiobooks.

Now, of course many of the traits that make men not put much effort into dating are themselves not very attractive. Most women are more attracted to smooth, confident flirts. A lot of women are going to be hesitant to date a man with issues about his romantic and sexual desires. Many women find being asked out itself attractive. And of course “dating apps emphasize physical attractiveness at the expense of other desirable traits” is irrelevant to you if you are primarily attracted to men with strong jaws and six packs (although you might still want to ask out gymcels).

But right now the dating market overweights those traits, relative to how much they matter for your long-term relationship happiness. Even if a man is romantically inexperienced, by the time you’ve been dating for a year, he’ll have exactly as much experience as any other man in dating you. An emotionally healthy man with internalized desexualization feels that way because he has never experienced a woman being attracted to him; if you show him that you’re attracted to him, he’ll believe it! And when you’re happily married, you’re just not going to care that much who asked whom out or whether the first date was kinda awkward.

I also want to point out some advantages of loveshy or romantically inexperienced men.

First, being the object of ten or twenty years of repressed sexual and romantic desire is both romantic and extremely hot. The sheer force of some loveshy men’s unleashed passion is indescribable. Not just sexually—although, yes, sexually—they are just so thrilled to be able to hold you and celebrate Valentine’s with you and tell you you’re beautiful and and and.

Relatedly, I’ve found that people who have spent years on the apps often wind up cynical, jaded, and prone to viewing all dating as a war between men and women. Many loveshy or inexperienced men, conversely, are earnest in a way that I almost want to describe as innocent. (Probably best to avoid ones who read dating discourse on X, which is the worst of both worlds.)

Second, as I have written before, the one of the most important factors in relationship happiness is having a delusionally positive view of how great your partner is. Loveshy or inexperienced men are far more likely to have a delusionally positive view of you, because as far as they know you’re irreplaceable, you saved them from a life of loneliness, and no one else has ever wanted them the way you do.

I think those men should ask me out.

I also think those men should ask you out but they keep not listening to me so now I am trying to address the other half of the problem.

Common Concerns

I would like a 6’ man who benchpresses twice his own bodyweight, earns six figures, is as emotionally mature as Gandhi, and has a giant cock. Will asking men out allow me to reach my goals?

I am not a miracle worker.

Taking advantage of this market failure will allow you to date somewhat above your “league” and to have an abundance of potential sexual/romantic partners. But very few men are the hero of a contemporary romance novel.
