Even if such men refuse to put any effort into dating, they will likely get scooped up by some other woman who has discovered the trick of asking men out. And you would have to meet hundreds of inadequate men before you find the Fitzwilliam Darcy of your dreams.

Consider seriously what is important to you and what isn’t. You might end up with a man with six pack abs who’s short, or a rich man with some interesting neurodivergences, or a tall man who can make up with certain inadequacies using his fingers.

In general, you will have an easier time with some preferences than others. Within my own niche, high IQ is basically free, while wealth and notable career success are not much harder. However, if you’re looking for muscles or a good fashion sense or a face that doesn’t look kinda dorky, you may end up having to compromise on other traits you would find desirable. (Some women I know have had very good outcomes through choosing men who are open to dressing well, and then buying all their clothes for them.)

If nothing will shift you from your desire for Buff Rich Big Dick Gandhi, I recommend trying to meet lots of men who don’t put much effort into dating, in order to maximize your chance of stumbling across such a person.

If he doesn’t put any effort into finding a partner, wouldn’t he not put any effort into me once we’re dating?

You know, you would think that’s true, but in my experience it’s really not.

Dating is stressful and horrible for many people. Talking to people on dating sites and going on first dates with strangers are the most excruciatingly awkward experiences our species has yet invented. Asking out people you know is terrifying. Getting rejected makes you feel like you’re about three inches tall. Very often, you put in a lot of effort and get nothing in return but a bunch of “I had a nice time, but I’m not feeling it” messages (if they don’t outright ghost you).

On the other hand, actually being in a relationship is fun. You get to do things like have sex and talk about your days and give each other emotional support and participate in each other’s hobbies and make sickeningly cute faces at each other while your friends all want to vomit. You can also more easily combine dating with other activities you want to do: you and your girlfriend can cook or go to parties or watch movies together, but none of these activities combine well with swiping on Tinder.

Many men are more interested in spending fun, fulfilling time with a woman they love than they are in doing a boring, soul-crushing activity with no obvious benefit.

I’m worried these men are misogynist or sexually entitled.

It is important to be aware that some men are loveshy because they are appalling misogynists and therefore no women want to date them. However, these men are easy to identify—if every other woman he’s ever met has figured out he’s an appalling misogynist, you can too.

In general, men who refuse to put any effort into dating have the same range of opinions about women as any other men: some are feminists, some are opposed to sexism but have various objections to modern feminism, some are decent people but have never really thought about gender issues, some believe strongly in gender norms and stereotypes, and some hate women. You should, of course, be actively screening for incompatible values and for general weirdness about women, but there is no need to take any unusual precautions in this regard.

Similarly, you should of course be alert to signs of sexual entitlement from any man when dating, but if anything the men we’re targeting are less likely than normal men to be sexually entitled. Men who experience internalized desexualization assume their sexual desire is unwanted and bothersome, and they don’t want to annoy any women by flirting with them, which is the opposite of sexual entitlement. In my experience, they often find women with clear boundaries reassuring—they know they’re not going to harm you by accident.

Be aware that some romantically inexperienced men have developed confused ideas of how dating works from some combination of social media, TV shows, and books. Some of these are obviously innocuous (e.g. Disneyfied “love at first sight”) but some can sound like red pill material (e.g. “women are only attracted to men who are taller than 6 feet”). Pay attention to whether he seems resentful of women or just (for example) sad about his own height. If his ideas seem more mistaken than hateful, and he’s willing to be corrected, I wouldn’t worry about it.

I’m worried that men who don’t ask me out don’t really like me.

I think this is the most common reason (besides “asking people out sucks for everyone”) that women don’t ask men out, and I understand the concern here. People are far, far, far more likely to say “yes” to a date than they are to ask the same person out. Saying “yes” is way less scary; if someone is interested in you, you often want to give them a chance, even if you’re not necessarily crushing on them right now. Many women don’t want to date someone who is giving them a chance. There’s a certain sense that “if he wanted to, he would.” Men are supposed to ask women out. If he doesn’t ask you out, he must not be attracted to you. And—especially if a man doesn’t have a lot of options—there’s a real risk he’ll slide into a relationship with you because it’s easy and better than being alone, even though he isn’t in love with you.

However, whether someone asks you out is only one piece of evidence about how much they like you, and it’s not even that good as evidence.

Imagine two men. Aaron crushes on a girl for six months before he finally works up the nerve to ask her out; since it takes a while for him to meet women he has a crush on, he asks out about one woman a year. Bob asks out any woman he is passingly attracted to, so he asks out one woman a week. If your social group is composed equally of Aarons and Bobs, you are literally forty-nine times more likely to be asked out by Bob than Aaron.

Now, this is an extreme case, and Bobs are actually quite rare. But the point stands that whether a man asks you out is evidence both about whether he is unusually interested in you and about whether he has read the Asking People Out Manifesto. Depending on how many Bobs are in your friend group, asking men out may even cause you to date men who are more attracted to you than you would date if you waited to be asked out.

Whether you asked a man out or the man asked you out, you should pay attention to all the information you have about whether he likes you. For example, how quickly does he respond to texts? Does he initiate text conversations? Does he make plans with you? Does he do things to make you happy? Does he do things to make you happy that are unusual for him, that he wouldn’t do for any random friend of his? Does he do things that are inconvenient for him to spend time with you or to make you happy? Is he affectionate (cuddles, kisses, compliments, sweet nothings)? Does he talk about your shared future together (whether that means talking about your future kids or planning a trip six months from now)? Does he make life plans with space for you? Does talking to him make you feel small, or humiliated, or like he wishes a Yeerk would enter your ear and make you a completely different person with the same face?

People will tell you whether they like you if you listen and pay attention. Most of the time, when you date someone who doesn’t really like you, the problem isn’t that they are failing to communicate; the problem is that you are doing wishful thinking. And wishful thinking is a problem whether or not the man asked you out.

I’m only attracted to assertive, dominant, extroverted men.

I will admit that my advice here works better if you are interested in men who are rather shy and passive, or at least don’t view shyness and passivity as a dealbreaker.

That said, there are extroverted, assertive, dominant men who are weirdly bad at putting effort into dating. Some men are extroverted in general but struggle to ask women out. Similarly, some men are assertive and dominant with other men or at work or while doing their hobbies, and are only passive in dating. With good partner selection, you can totally ask a man out and later find yourself hanging off his arm while a circle of supplicants waits breathlessly for his latest drop of wisdom, if that’s your kink.

If you have this set of preferences, and can see your way to being fine with handholding a man through the first few dates, I recommend having it as an adjunct strategy. Primarily choose to date men who ask you out, but if you encounter an assertive, dominant, extroverted man who happens to be single and not to notice any of your subtler flirtations, consider being direct.

I’m only attracted to men who make the first move.

Then don’t take my advice in this post. If you’re just not attracted to something, no one can argue you into being attracted to it.

That said, consider sending this advice to your friends, so that they ask people out, get into happy relationships, and leave more of the men willing to ask people out for you.

Target Audience

What kind of women should take this advice?

Some women will benefit more than others from taking advantage of this market inefficiency.

Of course, the more you’re attracted to the kind of men who refuse to put any effort into dating, the more useful this advice is. In particular, if you are particularly attracted to men who are passive, shy, adorably nervous and awkward, or undergoing a sexual awakening, and you don’t ask men out, you are an idiot.1

Within my own niche, I would recommend it highly to women who value men being intelligent, curious, well-read, and interesting. If your ideal date involves spending hours talking about history, programming, or the books you’ve been reading, you ought to ask men out.

If you are interested in High Status Men (TM), asking men out is a better idea if your idea of an extremely attractive high status man is “Nebula Award winner” or “multimillionaire because he was an early employee at a unicorn startup,” and a worse idea if your idea of an extremely attractive high status man is “professional basketball player” or “elected politician.” My advice is entirely useless if your idea of an extremely attractive high status man is “club promoter.”

Dating apps and “wait around until someone asks me out” both tend to advantage thin, feminine, conventionally attractive women, because (as discussed earlier) they both tend to weight easily visible traits like physical attractiveness over harder-to-see traits like kindness, intelligence, or emotional maturity. If you are plain, fat, or uninterested in doing beauty work, you will likely do better if you ask men out and then win them over with your charming personality.

I have asked a lot of men who refuse to put effort into dating to bluntly describe their sexual preferences to me, so I can help them get dates. From this, I have drawn the conclusion that these men tend not to care much about physical appearance, and tend to care more about personality and interests. You will likely do better if you are full of wonder about the world, like thinking about things, and have unusual hobbies. Female-dominated hobbies like fiber arts, baking, or writing fanfiction are terrible for meeting men, but work fine for this purpose.

Loveshy women will do better if they ask men out. I realize that this is difficult advice for loveshy women to put into practice—it is terrifying to ask people out, especially if you have little to no evidence that anyone has ever found you attractive—but I will walk you through how to do it in a later section. Loveshy people often make great matches for each other, but you will only be able to match each other if one of you does the asking!

Masculine or butch straight women definitely benefit from asking men out, although in this case it isn’t primarily because they’re taking advantage of the market inefficiency. Straight men who prefer masculine or butch women love it when a woman is direct, assertive, and sexually aggressive. Plus it is probably your natural style.

I’m a trans woman or nonbinary person assigned male at birth. Will this advice work for me?

Probably, yes.2

If you haven’t transitioned or are very early-transition, or your community tends to not be accepting of trans people, you should hesitate about hitting on straight cis men. You aren’t very likely to succeed, and you might provoke a man into a gay crisis, which could be humiliating for you and even potentially dangerous.

However, if people around you generally seem to treat trans women as women, and you are reasonably passable, I would urge you to ask out straight cis men you find attractive. Many more straight cis men than you think are open to transfeminine people. Many straight cis men are more interested in breasts, hips, soft skin, feminine facial features, and so on than they are in the vulva per se. In my experience, straight cis men who don’t put much effort into dating tend to be more flexible about cis/trans status—maybe because they tend to care less about physical appearance, or maybe because they tend to be motivated to get over the subconscious homophobia and cissexism that keeps many men from acknowledging their attraction to trans women.

In general, in trans-accepting environments, straight cis men who aren’t attracted to trans women aren’t going to hatecrime you. Indeed, they are most likely to feel uncomfortable about rejecting you, because they’re worried about hurting your feelings or accidentally misgendering you or making you feel unattractive. Be prepared for this; see “what happens if he rejects me?” below.

When dating straight cis men who aren’t chasers, you will generally have a better time if you don’t necessarily want to use your penis during sex (for example, because it makes you dysphoric). Even a lot of straight cis men who are attracted to trans women will never be the world’s biggest fans of penises. (If you have bottom surgery, of course, this makes the entire problem a nonissue.)

I know you girls are going to obsess about your incredibly male brow ridges or jawlines or midfaces or whatever.3 If strangers sometimes spontaneously call you “she” or “ma’am”, you are reasonably passable for these purposes and should feel free to hit on men whom you find attractive.

(Many of these men are also willing to date nonbinary people assigned female at birth, or early-transition/nontransitioning trans men. Similar considerations apply, although it’s worth watching out for signs that he sees you as a woman, which is not the recipe for long-term relationship satisfaction.)

How To Date Men Who Don’t Put Much Effort Into Dating

How do I find these men?

You will have very bad luck finding them on dating sites. Going on a dating site is putting concerted effort into dating, which is precisely what these men don’t do. Most of them have installed a dating app at some point, but they rarely messaged anyone and then promptly gave up. You have a low chance of catching one of them in the two months per half-decade they actually have the app installed.

Instead, you need to find them in your social circle. You may, especially if you’re a frequent reader of Thing of Things, already know many of these men! If your social circle is more than 60% male and many of these men appear mysteriously girlfriendless, consider the possibility that many of these men would quite like a girlfriend if one fell into their laps, and perhaps the person who falls into their laps can be you.

My personal experiences are mostly about a specific demographic of these men. Signs that your social circle also contains a concentration of them:

  • You live in a “tech hub” (the San Francisco Bay Area, Seattle, Boston).

  • Many of your friends are programmers, quant traders, STEM grad students, scientists, or people who work any job in which “working in industry” is a useful distinction as opposed to a tautology.

  • You’re into the kind of tabletop RPGs played by straight men, not the kind of tabletop RPGs played by queer people.

  • Anyone you know has or is working towards a PhD in physics.

  • Anyone you know has ever fondly reminisced about Mathcamp.

  • You are an effective altruist or rationalist (small portion of the population, large portion of my readers).

However, I suspect that this is more a reflection of my friends and blog readership, and less representative of all men who refuse to put effort into dating. I eagerly anticipate field reports from women about their own dating experiences with diverse groups of men who don’t put any effort into dating.

You might want to take my advice, but not have a concentration of these men in your social circle. In this case, I recommend getting into a “programmer hobby”: tabletop RPGs, board games, chess, Magic: the Gathering, speedcubing, writing science fiction or trashy webnovels, Ultimate Frisbee, rock climbing, Brazilian jiu jitsu, or anything you do at a makerspace. Running or cycling clubs are good if you’re in a tech hub but not otherwise. While Burning Man and social dance are both programmer hobbies, your odds are worse in these cases, because Burners and dancers are more likely to be comfortable with hitting on women. Again, this only reflects my own experiences; I hope people with other recommendations leave a comment.

A common mistake is to try to figure out whether a man struggles to ask women out before you hit on him. Once you have already determined that your social group has enough men who struggle to ask women out that this is a reasonable strategy, don’t bother obsessing over the prospects of any individual man. You will likely mistakenly assume that this man is so attractive that he must have gotten dates in the past, and therefore psych yourself out. Besides, even the men in these demographics who do get asked out tend to find being asked out a pleasant surprise, and to be kind and gracious about it.

How do I date these men?

You must ask them out.

There is no other way around it. These men are single because, for whatever reason, they won’t ask women out. The secret ingredient—the thing that lets you get these men when other women don’t—is that you are willing to ask them out yourself.

A common mistake women make is to look for the man to be flirtatious, or to show what pickup artists used to call ‘indicators of interest.’ Our target men will never do this, because they’re nervous and uncomfortable around women they’re attracted to, or because they’re concerned that even the mildest flirting is a form of sexual harassment. Look for general signs that a man likes you as a person—making an effort to talk to you at parties or social events, doing small favors for you, laughing at your jokes, the ordinary things that make you say “oh, this person wants to be my friend.” Don’t look for compliments, unusual levels of touch, strong eye contact, or anything else you would normally take as flirting.

Only ask a man out if you actively want to go on a date with him. If you’re unsure whether you want to go on a date with him, keep talking to him at parties or social events until you’re sure you’re up for at least a first date. If you want to go on a first date to get to know him, but aren’t sure whether you’d want a second, that’s fine.

Using some pretext, obtain the man’s contact information or get him alone. If you are struggling to think of a good pretext, “I’ve enjoyed our conversation, can I have your email/Discord?” and “it’s loud in here, want to go for a walk?” both work fine. Never ask a man out in front of other people—it will freak him out and make him feel pressured.

Then, say some sort of brief compliment. Ideally, choose something you like about him: “our conversation yesterday about the Roman Empire was the highlight of my night.” If you can’t think of anything, a vague “I like you” or “I enjoyed spending time with you” is fine. There are multiple schools of thought on whether to include “you’re cute” or similar. On the one hand, these men will completely miss any indicator of sexual interest more subtle than “you’re cute,” and including a “you’re cute” can simplify matters later in the date. On the other hand, if you’re unsure whether you’ll find the man appealing, leaving out the “you’re cute” allows you to retroactively make the hangout platonic seamlessly and without awkwardness.

Then, say “I would like to go out with you sometime.” In my experience, it is usually best to plan the date yourself according to your own preferences: say “let’s get coffee” or “I want to go see $movie” or “let’s go for a hike” or “come over to my place and I’ll make dinner” as you prefer. Choose whatever activity you like most without trying to please him. However, if you’re into the man planning the date, by all means leave it vague and allow him to come up with the activity.

On the date itself, you will need to make your interest clear and unambiguous. Three successful strategies are compliments, touch, and direct communication.

Direct communication is the simplest technique. Simply say “I really like you and I want to [go out on more dates with you]/[be your girlfriend]/[kiss you].” Very likely, only the most assertive and blunt women will want to use this technique, but it is useful if you’re too lazy for the other techniques.

A compliment is similar to the “you’re cute” you might have said while asking him out. Give a nonsexual but unambiguously romantic compliment: “you have a nice smile,” “you have beautiful eyes,” “I love your biceps,” “you’re cute,” whatever. A crass or sexual compliment (“nice ass”) will likely freak him out, while he might miss that a completely platonic compliment (“you’re so smart!”) is intended as flirtation.

If he is interested in you, he will normally return the compliment, often after a period of silence or unrelated conversation in which he is visibly working up the nerve to do so. Don’t be concerned if he repeats your compliment (“you also have a nice smile”). He might not know what kinds of compliments are okay, and is repeating yours because he’s sure that one is all right and not somehow sexual harassment. You can easily teach a man better compliment behavior once you’re dating (I will discuss this in more detail later).

Touch means making romantic physical contact with him. Begin with subtle, plausibly deniable touch, such as touching his shoulder to emphasize a point, hugging him as a greeting, or touching legs with him while you’re sitting on a couch. Observe whether he pulls away or reciprocates the touch. If he’s matching your level of touch, make a more romantic form of physical contact, such as holding hands or putting your head on his shoulder or chest. Again, notice if he reciprocates, pulls away, or escalates the touch himself. For example, if you put your head on his shoulder, he might put his face in your hair or even kiss your head in a matter he imagines is subtle but absolutely is not.

Unfortunately, many men who are inexperienced with women feel scared and uncomfortable when a woman touches them, even if they are very enthusiastic about the touch. So his body language might look like he doesn’t want to be there. If you notice a man has uncomfortable body language but he’s not pulling away, I recommend verbally checking in (”are you okay with cuddling?”).

If he has returned several compliments and/or you’ve been doing romantic physical contact for a reasonable period of time, you can kiss him. I usually find it least awkward to ask “can I kiss you?” but if he’s actually giving positive body language feel free to kiss him spontaneously. I have no personal experience with waiting for a man to kiss me but I imagine it taking for-fucking-ever for him to get brave enough to ask you; up to you.

What happens if he rejects me? I’m nervous.

If you ask men out, they might reject you.

Being rejected is scary and embarrassing for everyone. But remember that men turning you down for dates is a good thing. It means that you don’t wind up dating someone who is meh about the prospect of dating you. If a man isn’t physically attracted to you, has dreamed of nothing but being a dad since he was eight years old while you’re aggressively childfree, or is about to move to a different continent, you don’t want to waste six months on dating him while you find this out.

Many women don’t want to ask men out because they’re worried that men will say ‘yes’ without actually wanting to date them. Every man who rejects you has saved you from that fate.

When asking a man out, try not to think of the goal as getting a date. Think of the goal as letting him know about your feelings. As long as he knows what you feel about him, it’s a success. If you go on a date, it’s a success (date!). If he feels complimented but isn’t interested in you, it’s a success (you made someone you like happy and found out that the two of you aren’t compatible). If he’s an asshole, it’s a success (you have found out that he’s a jerk and won’t have to waste any more time with him).

Men who don’t put any effort into dating know that asking people out sucks. (That’s a major reason they don’t put any effort into dating.) Typically, they will try to reject you kindly, compassionately, and with concern for your feelings. Often, they’ll worry about making you feel unwanted or undesired. In my experience, it’s common for them to specifically reassure you that you’re attractive and that you’ll find someone else soon. In general, they don’t find being asked out annoying or burdensome; they feel happy and flattered that someone is interested in them, even if it’s someone they’re not interested in. Quite often, whether or not they want to date you, you wind up making their day!

Like most scary things, asking men out gets easier with practice. Your first time, you may very well have a panic attack. This is normal. Schedule a phone call or hangout with someone supportive for afterward, queue up some of your favorite TV show, or give yourself an extra dessert. Eventually, it’ll be easy.

What if he doesn’t know what to do while dating me?

Romantically experienced people enter dating with a lot of scripts about what’s supposed to happen when—who plans the date, what you talk about, who pays for the date, when you kiss for the first time, when you become exclusive or committed, when you open up about your pasts or your squishy feelings. Often, even late in the relationship, people rely on cultural scripts to answer questions like “are we allowed to have friends of the same gender?” or “when do we stop using condoms?” or “do we celebrate Valentine’s Day?” or “when do we move in together?”

Romantically inexperienced people don’t have these scripts. If you aren’t prepared, the first dates can wind up clumsy or awkward, because they have no idea what they’re supposed to do. But your partner’s romantic inexperience can also be an advantage for you, because they will tend to defer to you about what the scripts are, which means that the scripts for your relationship can be anything you want them to be.

Now, I am not saying that you should go against a man’s expressed preferences. Obviously, listen to him when he communicates his own needs and boundaries. But if you give obvious directions in early dating, he will tend to find this reassuring because now he has some guidance.

Most of the time, the best technique is to act decisively in accordance with your own preferences. As an example, imagine you don’t feel comfortable kissing on the lips until the third date. Romantically experienced men will usually interpret this preference as a sign that you dislike him or are totally asexual, which creates annoying stress and drama. But if you’re dating a romantically inexperienced man, you can simply kiss him on the cheek at the end of the date and say that you have a lovely time. Don’t apologize or try to explain; act like this is a perfectly normal thing to be doing, exactly what everyone does while dating. He will typically go along with you.

Similarly, if you prefer to split the check, simply take out your card and cover your half. If you think a man should plan the dates, say “what do you want to do next weekend?” If you’re polyamorous, talk about your partners in a calm, matter-of-fact way. If you prefer regular video calls when he’s on a work trip, say “I’m looking forward to your next video call.” The trick is to act like your preferences are the social norm and you expected him to know this all along.

Many women will feel selfish or uncomfortable about being this decisive. This is completely wrong. You are helping him. When you act this way, he feels relieved. Often, the whole reason that he hasn’t dated is that he doesn’t know how, and he’s terrified of making a mistake. Giving him clear scripts is a favor to him, and if you’re going to be doing it anyway, they might as well be whatever scripts you prefer.

You can also model the behavior you want to see from him. Romantically inexperienced men will typically take cues from you about dating. If you (say) make him breakfast in bed, you almost can see him go “oh! People who are dating are supposed to make each other breakfast in bed!” and expect a breakfast in bed next week. Similarly, if you hold hands with him in public, you can expect him to start grabbing your hand when you walk places. If you text him “good morning” every morning, you can expect him to start texting good morning. If you offer tactful constructive criticism about his sexual performance, you can expect him to start offering tactful but constructive criticism about yours.

Unfortunately, modeling only works for behavior that you also want to do, which makes it a bad fit for women with strongly gendered or otherwise nonreciprocal preferences. Men also might overgeneralize (“I should provide tactful constructive criticism about everything!”) or undergeneralize (“she compliments my smile, so I should specifically compliment her smile and not anything else”). But modeling is still a useful technique for your toolkit.

Finally, you can try direct communication. You should be doing this in relationships anyway, but it is particularly useful for relationships with romantically inexperienced people. If you have some preference, simply say it forthrightly, but without being critical: “I’d like it if you told me more about your day,” not passive-aggressive hinting, not “you don’t care about me!”, and not a lengthy tangle of words with so many caveats that he can’t tell what your point is. Often, praising good behavior (“I loved the picnic you planned last weekend!”) is better than criticizing bad behavior (“you never take me out!”). Remember, the poor behavior of a romantically inexperienced man is often ignorance, not malice.

The ability to set the scripts is very powerful. Part of the reason that age-gap relationships often end badly is that, if the older partner implies that people who really love each other have condomless sex or no woman lets her boyfriend have female friends or all men fly into rages, the younger partner has little evidence to the contrary. Experience-gap relationships can fall into the same problems. Feel free to set scripts that you like, but don’t abuse the power to create scripts that exploit him or make him unhappy.

How do I show this guy that I like him?

Many inexperienced men are used to no one being romantically or sexually interested in them, so they struggle to believe that you are interested in them just because you’re “dating them” and “telling them how much you love them” and “enthusiastically expressing your desire to have sex with them.” At best, this can be frustrating. At worst, it can cause serious relationship problems—you wind up not criticizing or disagreeing with him because you don’t want to set off a fit of insecurity, or having to limit your ordinary friendships and activities to keep him from being jealous.

The sine qua non of solving this problem is to only date emotionally mature people who are capable of deriving accurate beliefs like “my girlfriend wants to date me” from available evidence. I recommend this choice.

But you can help boyfriends who are only somewhat emotionally mature work out that you like them. I recommend clear, direct, and unambiguous communication.

By “clear, direct, and unambiguous communication,” I don’t necessarily mean saying “I really like you, want to have sex with you, and am happy to be dating you” (...although that sometimes helps). Instead, think of all the different ways you can communicate affection. Make a romantic playlist! Hold hands with him in public! Cuddle him to sleep! Give him specific, detailed compliments about whichever of his traits that you like! Write him a love letter! Tell other people how great he is in a situation where he can overhear!4 Plan dates you think he will like! Give him small presents that made you think of him! Ask thoughtful questions about his interests! Be really enthusiastic in bed! Cook for him! Read his favorite book!

Now, you will need to adjust this based on your individual style and personality. Some people aren’t the PDA type; other people dislike planning dates or being sexually forward. (...I do recommend reading his favorite book regardless.) But the idea is to signal fondness, affection, and appreciation in a way that is impossible to rationalize as you just being a generically nice person.

I understand that being emotionally demonstrative can be difficult for some people. To some people, it can feel vulnerable and embarrassing (“what if he thinks I’m a Stage Five Clinger?”). To other people, it can feel awkward and artificial (“what’s next, I stand below his window with a boombox that plays In Your Eyes?”). But I think the best solution for this kind of relationship insecurity is giving him undeniable evidence that you love him, that he makes you happy, and that you want to be with him.

In conclusion:

  • Many objectively attractive men don’t get dates because they won’t ask people out.

  • If you ask them out, you can date them.

  • Then you get a hot boyfriend.

  • Everyone wins.

1

I suspect connoisseurs of this sort are the minority, but if I convince even one straight woman with these preferences to take up asking men out, I will count my entire blogging career a success.

2

Straight cis men reading this who are not attracted to trans women: I am not the Trans Attraction Police. I have no power to force you to date trans women you don’t want to date, nor would I use this power if I could. But no one has a right to not be asked out by people they find unattractive. If you consider the matter, you would realize that “I have a right not to be asked out by people I’m not attracted to” is not in your best interest either. Please chill.

3

Incurably fembrained of you all.

4

I originally learned this technique from a book about parenting toddlers but it works great for relationships with adults too.

item.title: Strange mammals
item.description: Marsupial genitalia: exactly as much as you wanted to know
item.content:encoded:
By Hemlock Leaves

[This is a guest post from Mia of Hemlock Leaves.]

You can probably picture a baby kangaroo, with its little furry head peeking out of a pouch on its mother’s belly.

That’s not what a newborn kangaroo looks like.

Kangaroos have very short pregnancies which end as soon as their fetus has the absolute bare minimum functionality necessary to crawl from the birth canal to the pouch and start nursing. So this is what a kangaroo newborn looks like.

For people who don’t want to click on the (gross) link: a newborn kangaroo is a slimy pink shapeless blob, about an inch long, with bones, blood vessels, and organs visible through its nearly transparent skin. Its most recognizable feature is the relatively well-developed front legs, which it uses to grasp its mother’s fur when it climbs up to her pouch.

A newborn kangaroo doesn’t have hind legs yet. Its eyes and ears don’t work yet, but that’s fine, because it can navigate to the pouch by smell. It’s too tiny and hairless to maintain a stable body temperature, but that’s also fine, because its mother will keep the pouch warm. Its jaw muscles aren’t strong enough to hang on to its mother’s nipple, but again, totally fine, because the nipple will swell up as soon as it’s in the baby’s mouth and stay swollen for the next few months, making it physically impossible for the baby to detach. Its jaw muscles also aren’t strong enough to actually suck milk from the nipple, but everything is fine, okay, it’s fine, because the nipple will helpfully drip milk down its throat.

Kangaroos are marsupials. All of the over 300 species of marsupials—including koalas, possums, Tasmanian devils, and quokkas—follow the same reproductive playbook: a quick pregnancy produces a still-very-much-fetal baby, which needs to spend months developing in the pouch. Kangaroo newborns are actually pretty self-sufficient by marsupial standards. Some marsupial newborns don’t even have fully functional lungs yet, so they do most of their breathing through their skin.1

But most mammals aren’t like this. Most mammals—including humans, cats, zebras, pangolins, naked mole rats and over 6,000 more species—are what’s called “eutherians.” We have long pregnancies that produce large infants with working limbs and internal organs.

We eutherians diverged from the marsupials about 180 million years ago, before there were birds or flowers. Early marsupials lived all over the world, though they’re now concentrated in Australia, New Guinea, and South America.

We have some even more distant mammalian cousins: monotremes. Biologists don’t like it when you call monotremes primitive, but they do have a distinct vibe of being halfway between reptile and mammal. They run a bit colder than other mammals, in the high eighties Fahrenheit. They lay eggs. And although they do produce milk for their offspring, they haven’t totally figured out the nipple thing. Instead, monotreme mothers just secrete milk from glands on their skin—basically sweating it out—and let it pool on their bellies for their babies to lap up.

Monotremes historically lived in Australia, South America, and probably Antarctica. But they’ve been crowded out by marsupials and eutherians on those continents. Now there are just five species of monotremes left—the platypus and four types of echidna—in Australia and New Guinea.

So there are three mammalian lineages that have been independently evolving for hundreds of millions of years. Monotremes and marsupials are still recognizably mammals—they get pregnant and they feed their babies milk—but they do it in a very different way than we do. I’m going to talk about how these funhouse-mirror mammals work: what adaptations they need, what tradeoffs they face, what evolutionary doors have been opened or closed by their style of reproduction, why there are so few of them left. But first we need to talk about…

The plumbing

So that you’ll fully appreciate the madness that comes next, here’s a brief rundown on what a normal mammalian female reproductive system looks like.

So basically: two ovaries feed into a uterus. Sperm comes up and babies go down from the uterus through the vagina. Next to all that, but separate, is the urinary system. Pee goes down from the kidneys through the ureters to the bladder and then comes out through the urethra.

Okay, now here’s what a female marsupial looks like inside:

So they have three separate parallel vaginas, which meet back up at the top and hook up to the two (!) uteruses.

Why do you need three vaginas? Well, you need two side vaginas to carry sperm up to each uterus. But babies don’t come down through those vaginas. They come down through the third vagina in the middle.

(In some species, females are born with just the two side vaginas. When they’re ready to give birth, they grow the third vagina. The third vagina will stick around long enough to deliver the baby and then close back up until next time.)

Since each side vagina leads to a different uterus, males get the best chance of getting a baby if they can ejaculate into both vaginas at once. So some marsupials have forked penises.

(A lot of the same genes that build penises in male fetuses get reused for building clitorises in female fetuses. So, yes, some female marsupials have forked clitorises.)

The other weird thing with the marsupial genital situation is that the urinary system is tangled up with the reproductive system. The ureters go through the gaps between the side vaginas and the central vagina, and then they link back up with the bladder. From the bladder, pee goes out into the cloaca—which is also the entrance for the three vaginas. And the cloaca also hooks up to the digestive system. If you’re wondering what sorts of exciting infections you get if you have one exit for sex, pee, and shit—well, yeah, vets have to deal with this constantly.

But onwards! There are even jankier reproductive systems still ahead of us!

Female monotremes do all their business through one long tube:

Monotremes avoid tangling up their urinary and reproductive systems by having a very simple urinary system. Very very simple. Maybe too simple?

I spent a long time struggling to understand how exactly their urinary system worked. All the diagrams I saw showed both kidneys and a bladder but no kidney-to-bladder connection. Instead, the kidneys hooked up to the cloaca and the bladder also hooked up to the cloaca, at a different spot. But if pee goes directly from the kidney into the cloaca, then why doesn’t it immediately fall out of the cloaca?

As best as I can tell, the answer is that monotremes clench the muscles of their cloaca to hold the pee in and maneuver it up into the bladder until they’re ready to pee. So janky.

Male monotremes pee and poop through their cloacas, just like the females. They also store their penises inside their cloacas when they aren’t using them. When a male monotreme gets an erection, his penis will push out through his cloaca (probably picking up some of his fecal bacteria on the way out), then enter his partner’s cloaca (picking up some of her fecal bacteria), and then carry all that up her reproductive tract.

(Unlike with marsupials, I haven’t found any veterinary texts confirming my guess, but I gotta imagine that the UTI rate is devastating.)

In normal mammals, sperm travels from the testicles through a tube called the vas deferens that connects to the urethra, which carries the sperm out of the penis. Monotremes make the insane (but admittedly on-brand) choice of having the vas deferens drop semen into the cloaca, aka the General Purpose Pipe for Everything, and hope it somehow gets into the urethra.

I say “somehow” because we literally don’t know how the semen gets to the urethra, as opposed to going up one of the many other branches of the cloaca or just falling out the bottom of the cloaca. We have some educated guesses. Maybe ejaculations involve the cloaca muscles twisting to maneuver the semen into the urethra, in the same way that they get pee into the bladder? Maybe the penis physically blocks the cloaca exit to keep the semen in the cloaca and then the semen sloshes around in there until it gets to the urethra?

Fenelon et al. (2021) have lovingly documented the magnificently bizarre echidna penis, which divides into four separate heads (image here). Given that female echidnas only have two uteruses, four penises may seem excessive. And, in fact, only two of the four heads get used at a time. The extra two won’t even get erect.

It’s not totally clear why you’d evolve twice as much penis as you need and then only use half each time.

Males do switch off which half of their penis they use each time. Maybe this helps them have sex more frequently? That’s Fenelon et al.’s theory at any rate.

The other odd thing about echidna penises is the shape of the urethra. Most mammals just have a single straight urethra. Marsupials with forked penises have a urethra that forks once. Echidna urethras branch into four forks and then, near the tips, each fork branches again into dozens of tiny channels that spray out the semen like a sprinkler. I have no idea why this happens.

I couldn’t find much on the platypus penis, but based on pictures it appears to be bifurcated and also to have a lot of spikes around the tips. Spikes are surprisingly common in mammal penises,2 but the fork is a little strange given that female platypuses actually only have one working uterus. (The other uterus is vestigial.) Maybe the second fork is also vestigial? Or maybe platypus males, like their echidna cousins, alternate which side of their penis they use for increased stamina?

Pregnancy and lactation

I’ll again start with a refresher on how eutherian pregnancies work before I move on to the funhouse mirror versions. Sex happens: the male inserts his single-pronged penis into his mate’s one (1) vagina, deposits some sperm somewhere in her reproductive tract, and an egg gets fertilized. A week or so later, the embryo will attach into the side of the uterus and grow a placenta.

The placenta’s job is to pull food and oxygen from the mother’s blood and send them to the fetus through the umbilical cord. To do this, the placenta will have to get real cozy with the inside of the uterus. In most species, it presses right up against the blood vessels in what biologists charmingly call capillary intimacy. The intimacy gets even more intense in a few species, where the mother’s cells actually fuse with the placenta’s cells so that there’s a layer of cells with two nuclei and two sets of DNA, one from the mother and one from the baby.

Close contact between mother and fetus makes resource transfer very efficient. But it also means that eutherians have had to develop a lot of special adaptations to keep the mother’s immune system from freaking out about the rapidly growing, genetically distinct entity slurping nutrients from her bloodstream (you know, the exact threat vector that immune systems exist to defend against).

Monotreme mothers, in contrast, maintain a respectful distance from their unborn offspring. The embryo never attaches to the side of the uterus and instead floats freely for the whole pregnancy. To sustain their embryos, mothers will release nutrient-rich fluids into the womb, which is basically the equivalent of flinging handfuls of food in every direction in the hope that some of it will happen to land in your baby’s mouth. Consequently, monotreme embryos grow very slowly. After two weeks, the mother calls it a day, covers up the egg with a leathery eggshell, and lays it.

Marsupials do something in between. Marsupial fetuses spend most of the pregnancy floating in a bath of nutrient secretions, just like monotremes. Then, with about a week to go, the fetus gets a nagging feeling that maybe it’s forgetting something and belatedly jams its placenta into the side of the uterus. Even then, the implantation is pretty half-hearted. Most marsupial placentas don’t ever achieve capillary intimacy, and this probably limits how fast they can draw in nutrients from their mother. After a brief period of very daintily sipping from its mother’s bloodstream, the marsupial fetus is evicted. At this point, it’s the developmental equivalent of an eight- to ten-week human embryo.

Now, part of why marsupial fetuses are so underdeveloped is that marsupial pregnancies are super short. Eutherians have pregnancies that range from sixteen days to almost two years, but marsupial pregnancies cap out at 38 days, short enough to fit snugly within the mother’s ovulation cycle.

But a few eutherians have pregnancies just as short as the marsupials’—mostly very small eutherians.3 These eutherian mothers are still able to crank out way more baby in the same short pregnancy, because they let their developing fetuses implant sooner and (probably) suck in nutrients at a faster rate once implanted. Small marsupial mothers have newborns that are less than 0.2% of the mother’s mass, with litter sizes rarely exceeding 1% of maternal mass. Small eutherians routinely have babies that are 2-3% of the mother’s mass, with litters totaling a frankly horrifying 20% of maternal mass.

All this is to say: pregnancy is a very different animal for marsupial and eutherian mothers. Marsupial mothers basically don’t consume energy at a noticeably faster rate during pregnancy. They don’t get a baby bump. Some marsupial mothers reportedly give birth without appearing to notice.

Pregnancy for marsupials is so insanely cheap that some of them routinely birth way more babies than they can possibly nurse. Tasmanian devils are the worst offenders. Mothers give birth to twenty to thirty babies at a time. They only have four nipples in their pouch, and, remember, when a newborn marsupial latches on, it won’t let go for weeks. Tasmanian devil moms are literally physically incapable of caring for more than 20% of the babies they carry.

So, as soon as they come out of their mom’s cloaca, newborn devils have to race to claim a nipple before their siblings. The losers will dehydrate, freeze, or starve to death.

Marsupial moms make up for the short, low-commitment pregnancy with an extra long nursing period. You can see the difference by comparing matched pairs of marsupials and eutherians of about the same size occupying roughly the same niche. For example, Thomson’s gazelle (a eutherian) and the common wallaroo (a marsupial) are both mid-sized open-country grazers.4 The gazelle is pregnant for five months, but only nurses its baby for two months. The wallaroo zips through its pregnancy in a month, and then learns that it’s on the hook for a full year of nursing.

Because of these long lactation periods, marsupials tend to spend longer on each kid from conception to weaning, usually about 50% longer.

And marsupial babies change a bunch during lactation, so the content of milk also has to change. The nutritional needs an adorable furry baby that can move its limbs on purpose are different from the nutritional needs of a slimy thrashing fetus with creepy bulging balls of black tissue where the eyes should be.5 Early milk tends to be waterier and easy to digest. It contains a lot of iron, because marsupial newborns don’t have a liver capable of storing iron and so need their supply constantly topped off. Later milk has more concentrated fats and proteins to support a bigger and more active baby with a mature digestive tract.

One sidebar on pregnancy lengths: I said that marsupial pregnancies never last more than 38 days. That was a bit of a fib. There are never more than 38 active days of pregnancy. But some marsupials can pause their pregnancies a few days in and then unpause them weeks or months later.

Red kangaroos do this a lot. A day or two after a red kangaroo gives birth, she’ll mate again and get pregnant in whichever uterus didn’t just host a baby. But she won’t be ready to birth another baby right away, since her pouch will still be occupied for about seven months. So she’ll freeze her fetus after about two days of growth. Once her older child has left the pouch, she allows the fetus to resume growing and gives birth to it 31 days later. So red kangaroo pregnancies last anywhere from 33 days to 252 days.

Healthy female red kangaroos are almost constantly pregnant and it’s pretty common to find them caring for three rounds of offspring: a mature joey living outside the pouch but still nursing, a fetal joey living inside the pouch, and a suspended embryo waiting for the pouch to free up. One nipple will produce thin watery milk for the younger joey and another nipple will produce fattier milk for the older one.

Who is the best mammal?

Marsupials have a short, easy pregnancy followed by a long nursing period, and eutherians have a long, tough pregnancy followed by a short nursing period. So, who’s doing it right?

It’s tempting to say that it’s us. We’ve been thoroughly kicking marsupials’ asses for the last 60 million years or so. There are 6000 extant eutherian species and just 300 marsupial species. Eutherian mammals live on every continent, while marsupials are mostly restricted to Australia and South America. These are both fairly isolated continents—Australia is an island, and South America wasn’t connected to North America until pretty recently. And whenever eutherians have managed to cross over to Australia and South America, they’ve done pretty well for themselves:

  • About 30 million years ago, some rodents and monkeys floated across the Atlantic from Africa to South America on natural “rafts” made of vegetation.6 And just when the killer capybara-and-capuchin combo arrived, there was a big decline in marsupial species diversity in South America.

  • Around 3 million years ago, the Panama Isthmus rose up out of the ocean to connect the Americas, kicking off the Great American Biotic Interchange (GABI) as species crossed the land bridge. Before the exchange, all North American mammals were eutherians, while South America had lots of marsupials. This is basically the purest head-to-head match between the two clades that we’ve gotten, with each having the opportunity to spread into the other’s territory. And the result is...almost half of modern South American mammals are descended from North Americans who crossed over during GABI, but only about 10% of North American mammals are descended from South American species. And a lot of the successful South American immigrants were actually eutherian rodents—the descendants of the guys who floated over from Africa.

  • Around 3000 years ago, humans brought dingoes to Australia. At about that time, Tasmanian devils and dog-like marsupials called thylacines went extinct on mainland Australia (but stuck around on Tasmania, where there were no dingoes).

Each of these cases gets nitpicked a lot. Maybe climate change caused the decline in South American marsupials 30 million years ago? Maybe South American species disproportionately went extinct during GABI because they hadn’t coevolved with the fiercer North American carnivores? Maybe people told the thylacines that they were worse boys than the dingoes, and the thylacines all ran away to Tasmania in despair?7

None of the cases are individually clear-cut, but the overall pattern is pretty suspicious. And there’s not many examples of marsupials making it big in previously-eutherian territory—the only example I know of are the possums, who are doing pretty well in Central and North America.

There was a lot of academic discourse in the seventies and eighties about what happened. Many researchers pushed back on the frame that one mode of reproduction was superior to the other. Maybe eutherians and marsupials are just pursuing different, equally valid reproductive strategies, and the eutherians just got lucky or something.

I tend to be more sympathetic to the “eutherians are better” position. But to give the marsupials their fair shake, I’ll start with the benefits of the marsupial form of reproduction. We’ve already covered some of these: pregnancy is very easy for marsupials and birth is even easier.

Another possible advantage for marsupials is pelvic shape. Eutherians tend to have pretty sexually dimorphic pelvises—think about how human women tend to have wider hips than human men. This is because female eutherians need to be able to fit an entire baby skull through their pelvis. Male eutherians don’t have this constraint. They have whatever pelvis shape is best for running around, which usually means narrower hips. Since female marsupials give birth to teeny-tiny babies, they don’t need anything beyond a standard-width pelvis.

Marsupials might also have an easier time suddenly terminating reproductive effort, or, in less clinical terms, dumping a baby out of the pouch and leaving it to die. Marsupials terminate reproductive effort if the baby looks unhealthy or if they’re running out of food. Eutherians can and do miscarry fetuses under these circumstances, but having a late-term miscarriage is probably a lot harder on the mother than quickly turning her pouch inside out.

The most darkly funny version of this is the way that startled kangaroo and quokka mothers will sometimes dump their babies out of their pouch and sprint away. Not only will the mother run away faster if she doesn’t have to carry her pouchling, the abandoned baby is a softer target that distracts a potential predator while the mother gets a head start! I, uh, certainly hope that pregnant eutherians can’t replicate this strategy.

But there’s one area where eutherians have an advantage, and it’s an important one: how fast populations can grow.

Remember how eutherians spend less total time than marsupials on each batch of babies? This means that eutherian mothers can churn out litters at a faster rate. It also means that there’s less time between when a baby is born and when it’s ready to have babies of its own. Both of these contribute to faster population growth.

Now, marsupials can somewhat compensate for this by having more babies at a time. But—empirically8—the max growth rate of marsupial populations tends to be smaller than the max growth rate for eutherians.

Obviously, populations aren’t growing at their maximum rate most of the time. But the ceiling still matters. Populations that are capable of growing really fast can bounce back more easily from a sudden shock and are better at quickly expanding into new territory.

All the marsupial advantages—easy births, narrow hips, casual child abandonment—are real. But when a land bridge rises or a fresh continent appears, it’s pretty hard to beat the ability to make more baby even faster.

Many marsupials

Here’s one last hypothesis about why there are fewer marsupial species. Remember, right after being born, marsupials need to be able to climb up their mother’s stomach and crawl into the pouch. This means that they have to be born with strong front legs capable of gripping and climbing. And maybe—the hypothesis goes—that requirement constrains the possible set of front legs they can have once they’re adults. It’s tough to grow a climbing claw and then regrow it into a wing or a flipper or a hoof. Maybe that’s why we don’t have marsupial bats or seals or horses.

I don’t really buy this one. For one thing, as Andrew Cockburn points out, not all marsupial newborns actually climb into the pouch. Newborn bandicoots dangle on their umbilical cord until their mother manages to swing them onto a nipple, which is quite an image. Tasmanian devils are apparently “ejected” directly from their mother’s cloaca into her pouch (also quite an image).9

And the shape of the limb at birth doesn’t fully determine the shape in adulthood. Some marsupials do lose the climbing claws and grow totally new structures.

Yes, it’s true that there aren’t any marsupial bats or seals or horses. But marsupials have managed to diversify quite a lot—here are a few examples.

Let’s start with my favorite: the Tasmanian devils. “Tasmanian devil” is actually one of the more flattering names that have been given to the species. (Other names include “Beelzebub’s pup” and the early species name Sarcophilus satanicus, which is neo-Latin for “Satanic flesh-lover.”) They have a bit of a reputation for viciousness, probably because of their scary-sounding howls and all the cannibalism10 and maybe also the thing where sometimes ranchers will come out in the morning to find the skeleton of a cow, picked clean to the bone, with a few devils in a food coma napping inside the rib cage.11

Tasmanian devils are the largest surviving marsupial carnivores, at about 25 pounds. You can think of them as basically marsupial hyenas—good hunters and excellent scavengers. They have extremely powerful jaws, which can bite down as hard as a dog four times their size. They mostly use their jaws to crack open bones, but they’ve also been known to chew through steel wires. They eat a lot, both in the sense that they can wolf down 40% of their body weight in a sitting, and in the sense that they aren’t at all picky. Objects that have been found in devil droppings include: part of a woolen sock, a wallaby foot with bit of snare wire still attached, a pet collar, twenty-seven echidna quills, stock ear tags, the head of a tiger snake, half a pencil, an owl foot, a cigarette butt, and bits of tinfoil, plastic, styrofoam, and steel wool.12

Marsupial moles, on the other hand, live underground in the Australian desert. They’re great diggers with big front claws. The sandy desert soil is too loose to dig permanent burrows, so marsupial moles “swim” underground, digging a temporary tunnel in front of them and letting it collapse behind them (marsupial mole mothers have backward-facing pouches, so that the pouch doesn’t get full of sand as the mother tunnels around). They don’t need to come up to breathe, since their slow metabolism lets them get by on air trapped between grains of sand.

No marsupial has evolved wings, but sugar gliders have gotten closest. They have wide “flying” membranes between their legs which let them glide through the air from tree to tree—as many as 150 horizontal feet in a single glide!

I’ve mentioned the uncannily canine marsupials called thylacines, which had long narrow snouts and pointed ears (although Science has investigated and unfortunately informs us that they were unable to wag their tails). They usually ran around on all four legs but also apparently could hop like a kangaroo on their hind legs (!). Sadly, thylacines went extinct in 1936, although some people are trying to fix this and resurrect them from preserved tissue samples.

Speaking of marsupials that are no longer with us, the prehistoric Australian roster included a lion-sized carnivore (Thylacoleo carnifex) and a rhino-sized mega-herbivore (Diprotodon) that roamed the plains in large herds.

Also giant kangaroos! These guys weighed over five hundred pounds. Some people think that the largest kangaroos wouldn’t have been able to hop and would have instead strolled upright on two legs like a human.

Coda: monotremes are just really weird

There was a lot of academic discourse in the seventies and eighties about the relative advantages of the marsupial and eutherian modes of reproduction. Academics wrote many, many papers accusing other people of thinking marsupials were “inferior” mammals or defending themselves from such accusations. Strangely, no one stood up for the monotremes.

I’m not going to stand up for them now. I think it’s pretty likely that monotremes are in some sense worse—less adaptable or less fertile—and it’s not just bad luck that their diversity has diminished and their continents have been steadily taken over by the marsupials and then the eutherians.

But I love strange mammals, and so I’m grateful that the monotremes have hung on long enough for us to study them. In celebration, I’ll finish this post with some of my favorite monotreme facts.

  1. Monotremes can sense nearby electric currents. For platypuses, this is the main form of sensory guidance they use while hunting underwater, since they shut their ears, eyes, and nose before they dive.

  1. Platypuses are one of the few biofluorescent mammals. They look like this under UV light.

  1. Monotremes also have a different sex chromosome system than other mammals. Marsupials and eutherians have two sex chromosomes (XX or XY), but female monotremes have ten Xs and males have five Xs and four or five Ys (depending on the species), which is crazy! I don’t think I’ve ever heard of a species with that many sex chromosomes.

    And as far as I can tell, they evolved this chromosome system totally independently from other mammals. Eutherian and marsupial sex chromosomes match each other—they have similar genes in similar orders—which suggests that they both developed from the same chromosome in the common ancestor of eutherians and marsupials. But none of the monotreme sex chromosomes match the eutherian/marsupial chromosomes in this way. If anything, they kinda look like     bird sex chromosomes. Weird!

  1. Platypuses are also one of the few venomous mammals. Male platypuses have venomous spurs on their hind limbs, which they use during mating season to fight off rival males.

  1. Echidnas have a much more civilized mating ritual, in which males will form an orderly single-file line behind a female and follow her around for hours or days. The suitors organize themselves by size, with the biggest at the front of the line—the female will have sex with whoever’s at the head of the queue when she’s ready to mate. Naturalists have seen lines of up to eleven males behind a single female.

  1. But platypuses make up for their lack of an adorable courtship ritual by having very adorable sex. The couple mates in water for up to 20 minutes at a time. There isn’t any pelvic thrusting or anything. The pairs’ genitals lock together and then the female swims forward slowly, towing the male behind her, while the male strokes her back and head.

1

Their small size makes this strategy viable. Smaller animals have a greater surface area to volume ratio: surface area controls the rate at which they can intake oxygen and dispose of carbon dioxide through their skin, while volume is proportional to the total amount of cells and thus the overall demand for oxygen. See J. B. S. Haldane’s classic essay On Being the Right Size for more on this and other tradeoffs that animals face at different sizes.

2

It’s not totally clear what the evolutionary advantage of the spikes is.

One clue is that penis spikes often happen in species where females only ovulate after they’ve had sex. So maybe the spikes are there to make sure that the female really knows that sex is definitely happening (source: owwwwww) and it’s time to release some eggs? Or maybe the spikes are there to scrape out the sperm left by the female’s previous mates? Or maybe the spikes hook into the vagina wall and make it harder for the female to pull away, which lets the male ejaculate for longer?

If you’re thinking that it sounds pretty unpleasant to be on the receiving end of a spiky penis, yep, it often is. But fairly adversarial reproductive strategies can and do evolve, and spiky penises are far from the worst.

3

Eutherian pregnancy length is strongly correlated with adult size. Interestingly, marsupial pregnancy length is pretty weakly correlated with adult size.

4

That example and a lot of arguments in this section comes from this excellent paper.

5

If you can’t tell, I’m watching a time-lapse video of a kangaroo infant as I write this.

6

Africa and South America were closer back then, and the oceans were lower, but the journey still would have involved traveling ~1000 miles over the open sea.

7

Okay, fine, that’s not the real alternative hypothesis. The other explanations are some combination of:

  • Humans hunting the thylacines and Tasmanian devils and/or indirectly causing ecosystem changes that disadvantaged the marsupial carnivores. Humans had been in Australia for tens of thousands of years before the introduction of the dingo, but their population probably increased a lot about 3000 years ago.

  • Climate change, which caused more frequent droughts.

8

From Thompson (1987), which is investigating how quickly a population could grow under basically ideal conditions---i.e., if each female reproduced continually starting at the typical time of female reproductive maturity and finishing at the typical time that females stop reproducing, each time producing a litter of average size. Because he’s trying to estimate the maximum possible growth rate, he mostly sticks to data from animals in captivity with unlimited food, which is of course not the typical situation.

9

I wonder how many of the babies that get fired blindly out of the cloaca actually land in the pouch. Wait, is this why Tasmanian devils have such an excessive number of babies?

10

Tasmanian devil adults regularly eat juvenile Tasmanian devils. The first attempt to breed devils in captivity ended when the dad ate his offspring. (In the wild, Tasmanian devil fathers are long gone by the time their kids are born, so they’re not really adapted to avoid eating babies they encounter. The zookeepers hadn’t figured this out and kept the dad in the same enclosure as his mate and her children).

11

To be clear, devils don’t kill cows. They just opportunistically eat cows that died of natural causes.

12

This list and most of the Tasmanian devil facts in this section are from David Owen and David Pemberton’s book Tasmanian Devil: A Unique and Threatened Animal.

item.title: Mindful posting
item.description: It is important, for the preservation of American democracy and maybe the world, that the Democrats take the House and Senate in November.
item.content:encoded:
It is important, for the preservation of American democracy and maybe the world, that the Democrats take the House and Senate in November.

(If you don’t agree with me about this claim, I wrote a blog post about it here.)

I recommend donating to high-value political candidates. But I want to bring to everyone’s attention an equally important thing they can do to improve Democrats’ chances in November: practice mindful posting.

“Mindful posting” is making sure, whenever you post about American electoral politics, that you post only content that is going to persuade your American followers to vote for a Democrat in November.

Half of all U.S. adults say they get news often or sometimes from social media. Social media is less popular as a news source than search, TV, or news websites, but more popular than podcasts, email newsletters, or AI chatbots.1

But if you want to reach a significant number of people through TV news or news websites, you will need to be a professional journalist. Similarly, if you want to reach a significant number of people through your podcast or email newsletter, you will need to be an obsessive weirdo who responds to “how was your day?” with “well, Cartoons Hate Her posted about this amazing genderslop—” But a normal person can talk to hundreds or even thousands of people through posting on social media.

Most people, when they think about raising awareness of their candidate, think about phonebanking or canvassing. But a single Instagram post can easily reach as many likely voters as hours of phonebanking or days of canvassing—and they’re more likely to listen to you instead of going “sorry! Aliens just landed in my backyard! First contact! Literally right now! Gotta go!”

The problem is that canvassing and phonebanking come with scripts designed by high-paid consultants and pollsters who at least in theory know how to appeal to undecided voters. But your social media messaging comes from you. Unless you think about it, you’ll post whatever is most emotionally satisfying to you, which might well be:

  • Despair about how America is irreversibly descending into fascism and everything we do is just amusing ourselves on the way to the death camps and/or Skynet drones.

  • Murderous revenge fantasies about Donald Trump, J.D. Vance, Elon Musk, ICE employees or undecided voters.

  • Guilt-trips about how undecided voters are universally moral morons who in a just world would be deprived of all democratic rights as they have proven themselves unworthy to wield them, but in our fallen world can redeem themselves partially by voting Democrat this time.

  • Rage at people whose political opinions are completely indistinguishable from yours to 99.9% of the population.

  • Arguments that the true solution to America’s problems is a radical, unprecedented change that is utterly unappealing to everyone who doesn’t read your favorite Substacker.

None of these are convincing to undecided voters.

I’m not saying that you should never despair, rage, guilt-trip strangers, or argue in favor of radical and unappealing changes. I myself have been known to harbor the occasional violent revenge fantasy about Elon Musk. But the appropriate audience for these sentiments is a group chat with fifty people who already agree with you, a locked social media account, or if you must Bluesky in December.

It’s difficult to generalize about how to engage in mindful posting, because people’s followerships are different. If your followers are mostly evangelical Christians who vote straight-ticket Republican, you’re going to need different content than if your followers are mostly leftists who think Trump and Biden are indistinguishably evil. No advice I can give you will outperform thinking seriously about the undecided voters in your own audience.

However, in terms of general strategy: voters care most about the economy, so it’s probably best to prioritize the economy. The Democratic Party is doing pretty well on most issues:

A different poll—this one of voters in swing districts—shows a somewhat different picture:

[The Democrats] perform better on the economy (+7), dealing with inflation (+8), lowering gas prices (+12), dealing with international trade and tariffs (+9) and addressing corruption in Washington (+7). Republicans have an advantage only on the issue of immigration (+5). And perhaps most notably, these voters trust Democrats to address policies related to data centers by a 10-point margin, 47% to 37%.

My advice is to prioritize posting about health care, which has long been the Democrats’ best issue, as well as the economy. Israel/Palestine is one of Democrats’ best issues, but I’m not sure what the American public even understands Democrats’ position on Israel/Palestine to be, so maybe be cautious about that one. I would post about immigration carefully: brutal ICE raids on sympathetic targets yes, open borders and “No One Is Illegal On Stolen Land” no. I have no idea how to interpret the findings about AI but probably if you’re inclined to post a lot about AI your top concern isn’t whether Democrats win in November.

I would recommend being positive about the Democrats. The Democrats are unpopular, just not as unpopular as Trump—which is a fragile position going into the midterms. In particular, when posting about corruption in Washington, I’d recommend listing off positive things about Democrats and not just the endless litany of Trump authoritarianism and crimes.

For the love of God, please save being weird and offputting about the culture war until December. There will be plenty of time for trans people to freak the mundanes when we don’t have an aspiring dictator in the White House.2 For now, make like the 2010s gay rights movement: if you’re going to talk about trans rights, be wholesome and sympathetic.

Of course, these are generalizations, and you know your own audience best. If most of your followers are libertarian, posting a lot about open borders and very little about healthcare might be exactly the right move. Maybe posting freaky shit about trans people will make you seem more credible to your leftist followers when you tell them to vote.

Some people might object that this is Lying. To be clear, I don’t mean that you should say things you don’t believe to be true. But your social media feed is not an endless stream of every thought that passes through your head. You exercise some curation—to respect other people’s privacy, to avoid oversharing, not to get dogpiled by people with poor reading comprehension, to be diplomatic about longstanding disagreements with your friends, not to cause problems for your employer or your jobhunting. All I’m saying is that you can additionally add the filter “does this make the Republicans more likely to win in November?”

I don’t mean to imply that everyone has to post about American electoral politics.3 Social media is (allegedly) supposed to be fun. If you’d rather talk about your cat, by all means post cat pictures. But if you’re going to be posting about American electoral politics anyway, you can do a remarkable amount of good by trying to persuade people.

1

Three times as many people get news from email newsletters as get news from AI chatbots! Substackers stay winning.

2

Again, totally fine to post about how vulvas are a male body part, everyone should be given puberty blockers, and we need to abolish gender—in your group chat, on your locked social media feed, or in December.

3

Thing of Things itself is unlikely to produce articles titled “Tariffs Make Prices Go Up” or “The Iran War: Not Just A Humanitarian Crisis, But Also A Reason Things Are Slightly More Expensive.” Unless you guys are really enthusiastic about the prospect, I guess.

item.title: Hunting is sometimes good for animals
item.description: Much more than you wanted to know
item.content:encoded:
Animal advocates typically oppose hunting. Anti-hunting activism is one of the few popular interventions to improve wild-animal welfare for the animals’ own sake (rather than for the sake of conservation or human benefit). Unfortunately, I think anti-hunting activism is often misguided.

Some popular kinds of hunting present few direct welfare issues. Indeed, they plausibly cause a significantly less painful death than the animal would otherwise have. I also think that hunting could potentially be a useful management tool in ecosystems managed to improve wild-animal welfare, and I think it’s bad to dismiss this tool out of hand because we assumed without evidence that it’s bad for the animals.1

Now, the study of hunting and animal welfare has a lot of methodological issues. For one thing, almost all the rigorous studies are conducted by a single researcher, Jordan Hampton.

Over the course of my research, I have developed a parasocial relationship with Jordan Hampton. He is the only person writing papers about hunting that aren’t stupid. For example, instead of looking at the injuries on dead animals’ bodies and trying to figure out how much they suffered, Jordan Hampton pioneered the innovative technique of actually going with hunters into the field, watching them kill animals, and writing down how long it took the animals to die. Our entire civilization’s understanding of the welfare of hunted animals rests on the shoulders of one Australian.

Anyway, if it turned out that Jordan Hampton was faking his data or something, we’d be totally fucked.

The other big methodological issue is that “hunting” refers to wildly different activities. It is “hunting” to shoot a deer who never notices you were there, dies instantly, and would have starved to death otherwise because deer are overpopulated in the area. It is also “hunting” to terrify an entire herd of feral pigs by shooting at them from a helicopter, aim poorly, and condemn four animals to lingering painful deaths and one escapee to lifelong chronic pain. Obviously, these have very different effects on the animals!

In particular, studies typically focus on large mammals. It’s unclear how the results generalize to birds, small mammals, or other taxa, and it’s likely that they have different experiences than large mammals do. And because Jordan Hampton is responsible for most of the useful papers in this area, we know very little about hunting and animal welfare on continents other than Australia.

How Is Hunting Bad For Animals?

This might seem like a stupid question—the animal is dead, duh. But if we’re going to think through what the harms of hunting are, we need to get clear on what the harms of hunting might be.

First, it might be wrong to kill an animal for non-consequentialist reasons—for example, maybe it’s always wrong to kill a sentient being.
