This is an interesting philosophical question that I’m not going to talk about in this article, since presumably you can lay out the considerations for and against it yourself.

Second, if an animal dies prematurely, she wouldn’t have all the experiences she would have if she had gotten to live longer. Some of these experiences are likely pleasurable, like sex, play, eating, grooming, and parenting. Some of these experiences are likely painful, such as injury, starvation, excessive heat or cold, or social rejection. It’s, uh, controversial among wild-animal welfare advocates whether wild animals in general have lives worth living.2 I don’t know by how much hunting typically shortens a wild animal’s life; as far as I can tell, no one has ever studied this.

Similarly, in social species, other animals may miss the prematurely killed animal (even if they don’t have an understanding of “death” per se). If the prematurely killed animal was a parent, their death might threaten their young. Again, I don’t know by how much hunting typically shortens a wild animal’s life, so it’s hard to get a sense of the scope of this problem.

Third, dying itself is typically painful. I will discuss this in the section ‘Pain of Death.’

Fourth, the experience of being hunted may cause fear and stress. I will discuss this in the section ‘Stress.’

Fifth, there are various flow-through effects related to hunting. For example, hunting may decrease the population of the target species, which has various effects on the experiences of the survivors and other species in the ecosystem. Hunters might advocate for certain policies, such as vaccinations, predator control, or keeping game species populations high. Hunting might decrease human respect for wild animals or increase human willingness to intervene in nature. These flow-through effects might well have a larger effect size than hunting itself, but I don’t know how to think about them so I’m going to ignore them.

Pain of Death

One way to measure the pain a dying animal experiences is to measure the amount of time it takes for the animal to become unconscious. Intuitively, if an animal becomes unconscious immediately, she likely suffers little, if at all. Conversely, if an animal takes hours to die, she will likely suffer a great deal.

(Mostly Large) Mammals

Substack doesn’t have good embedding of tables, so after some woe I have decided to include a link. Here’s an excerpt from the table, just so you get an idea:

Time to death is defined as the interval from the first shot being fired until the time the animal falls and doesn’t move. This isn’t perfectly accurate—an animal might be unable to move but still alive. However, since most hunting occurs at a distance, it’s not practical to use some more accurate metric. Death or unconsciousness probably follows within a few seconds at most.

Instantaneous death rate is the proportion of animals for whom time to death is zero; these animals can be presumed to experience little or no suffering. A clean miss was fired, but didn’t injure the animal; note that some reported “clean misses” might have actually hit the animal, but observers couldn’t see it. Animals injured then killed were shot non-fatally at first, then shot additional times, killing them. Animals which escape wounded were shot but not killed; presumably they either die of their injuries hours or days later or are disabled in the long term.

The rows don’t necessarily add to 100% because sometimes an animal takes a while to die but isn’t shot multiple times in the process.

Unless noted, all studies are of animals that were stalked (pursued stealthily on foot by a hunter).

General conclusions:

  • With the exception of rabbits, animals shot from a helicopter, and red deer, upwards of 80% of hunted animals die instantaneously.3

    • Rabbits are the smallest animals studied so presumably the hardest to aim at? Similarly, presumably it’s hard to aim well from a helicopter?

    • I don’t understand why red deer have relatively bad instantaneous death numbers though.

  • Of the remaining animals, median time to death was generally less than a minute.

  • In all species except rabbits, less than 10% of animals escape wounded.

  • In some species, no animals escape wounded.

In conclusion, the deaths of hunted large mammals are usually quick and clean. I am somewhat concerned about rabbits.

Birds

The evidence about bird hunting, conversely, is scanty.

A study of nine bird species in Northwestern Europe found that 17% carried embedded shotgun pellets, with larger species being more likely to have embedded shotgun pellets. Bewick’s swans had the highest rate of embedded shotgun pellets (33%) while dark-belled brent geese had the lowest (4%). Adults had a higher rate of embedded shotgun pellets than juveniles. Most individuals with an embedded pellet had only one embedded pellet, but one greylag goose had 28 pellets (!). Unfortunately, this study doesn’t give us information about whether birds with embedded pellets experience impairment or chronic pain, but it does suggest that birds escaping wounded are quite common.

The rate of mourning doves shot but not recovered is highly variable over time, ranging between 18% and 50% and averaging about 25%. Hunters, however, report about 30% fewer doves shot but not recovered—about 15% to 18% of doves. A study of pink-footed geese found that at least 0.7 birds were wounded per bird killed. If hunters use lead shot, about 23% of hunted ducks and goose escape wounded. Conversely, after a lead ban, only about 15% of hunted ducks and 10% of hunted geese escaped wounded.

In a population of common eiders, 29% of adults, 18% of immature birds, and 15% of juveniles had lead shot embedded within them. Embedded birds had 1 to 7 pellets, with juveniles typically having more pellets within them than older birds. Wounded and unwounded birds had similar body condition, although unwounded juveniles had more fat than wounded birds of the same age. Since juvenile common eiders make up the majority of harvested common eiders, this probably means that wounded juvenile common eiders have less fat because of their injuries, and so they die before they grow up. Among older common eiders, injuries don’t seem to cause poor body condition in the long term (although they might cause chronic pain or other welfare issues).

My guess here is that birds escaping wounded is very common (more than 10% and less than half?). Many birds seem to survive a while with wounds. I’m not sure how much of a serious welfare concern this is.

Stress of Death

Acute Stress

The experience of being hunted (separately from the experience of dying) might cause an animal suffering. To figure out whether an animal experiences suffering when it dies, researchers typically look at biomarkers of acute stress:

“Acute stress” is a cluster of physiological responses that prepares the animal for dealing with certain situations that are, well, stressful. Acutely stressed animals are stronger, have more energy, and think faster. The animal’s body draws energy away from less urgent things—eating, digesting, trying to seduce other animals, exploring—and towards more urgent things, like fighting or running away. You’ve felt acute stress before: you feel it when you are running to catch a bus, making a speech in front of a crowd, talking to someone you want to impress, or half-watching your kid and half-watching TV and then you realize you haven’t heard anything for the past five minutes.

Acute stress doesn’t necessarily mean an animal is unhappy. The acute stress response is a preparation for action, not an indicator of poor welfare. An animal might experience an acute stress response when having sex, running towards some tasty food, or even playing, without actually being unhappy in any way. However, we can make the shrewd guess that animals who were experiencing an acute stress response while being hunted weren’t doing so because of how ecstatically, orgasmically happy they are about being shot at.

Shot animals consistently experience less acute stress than animals caught in traps (see Marks, 2010; Jacobson, Kirkpatrick, and McGinnis, 1978; Hamilton and Weeks 1985; Westhoff et al., 2022). In general, trapped animals show signs of dehydration, intense activity, and an acute stress response, which is consistent with a terrifying, slow, and painful death. Shot animals don’t show these signs nearly as strongly.

In general, stalked animals (that is, animals pursued stealthily on foot by a hunter) show very few signs of acute stress (see Bradshaw and Bateson, 2000; Gentsch, Kjellander, and Röken, 2018; Cockram et al, 2011). Although these studies are generally of wild ungulates, I think they generalize, because stalked animals might not realize that they were being hunted until they were shot. Red deer stalked by more than one hunter tend to experience more stress than animals stalked by only one hunter, presumably because they’re more likely to notice that they’re being hunted; again, I expect this generalizes.

In roe deer but not moose, red deer, or fallow deer, battue (the use of beaters to drive the animal towards the hunter) causes more stress in hunted animals than stalking does.

Hunting animals with a helicopter is stressful for the animals. Indeed, in red deer, helicopter hunting is the only form of culling more stressful than death in a slaughterhouse.

Hunting with dogs is also stressful for animals. For example, in deer, hunting with dogs is associated with higher levels of stress than stalking. In a study of mountain hares, blood cortisol levels were 6.6 times higher in mountain hares hunted with dogs than in mountain hares hunted without dogs. (Some hares hunted without dogs were chased briefly, while others were shot without a chase.)

In a study of wild boar, a driven hunt, in which a line of beaters with dogs chases boar towards stationary hunters, was more stressful than an enclosure hunt, which also involves beaters and dogs but in a smaller, confined area. The least stressful option was a high-seat hunt, which is the equivalent of stalking for boar—a single hunter quietly waits for a single, unsuspecting animal. Another study also found that a high-seat hunt was less stressful than a driven hunt. The difference in cortisol levels was statistically significant at p < 0.0001, which is really the sort of p-value I associate more with physics than with research into the behavior of macroscopic particles.

In another study, about half of boar killed in drive hunts had a cortisol level that indicates trauma, while 40% had a normal cortisol level. (A boar with a normal cortisol level might still be experiencing acute stress, just less extreme.)

A particularly striking study compared red deer hunted with dogs to red deer euthanized because it was inhumane to allow them to continue suffering that intensely. The biomarkers indicate that the hunted red deer were more stressed than the euthanized red deer. Now, this is an unusual case in many ways—red deer don’t run long distances in the wild, and red deer hunts regularly last for over an hour. But I think this study should provide convincing evidence that some forms of hunting are frankly sadistic and should be banned in a civilized society.

However, it is inappropriate to generalize from that study to all hunting. To be perfectly frank, it is difficult to imagine that much suffering is experienced by an animal that doesn’t realize that she’s being hunted until a bullet goes through her head, killing her within a few seconds. We should all have deaths that painless!

In social species, hunting with dogs or helicopters is presumably also stressful for the animals who didn’t get shot at, but as far as I know no one has studied this.

Chronic Stress

One study looked at biomarkers of chronic stress—that is, the long-term stress that is far more closely associated with poor welfare. Unlike acute stress, chronic stress is always a welfare issue; human equivalents are poverty, abuse, depression, and grief.

The study looked at levels of cortisol and its metabolites in the hair, feces, and blood of red deer hunted using dogs. The blood samples reflect the animal’s immediate physiological state; the fecal sample, its state over the past week or so; and the hair sample, its state over the past few weeks to months.

In general, blood cortisol levels decreased over the course of the hunting season, indicating some level of acclimation to the stressor (although without a control group it’s impossible to say how stressed the animals were even after acclimation). Fecal cortisol metabolites were higher in samples from hunted deer than in samples picked up noninvasively from an area where hunting isn’t allowed. Hair cortisol concentrations increased gradually over the course of the hunting season.

These results suggest that red deer hunted with dogs are in a state of persistent chronic stress. However, unless this study’s results are replicated in other species and with other types of hunting, it is impossible to determine whether the problem is hunting in general, or hunting red deer with dogs specifically. (You will note that I previously called “hunting red deer with dogs” a sadistic form of hunting that should be banned in any civilized society.)

Another study shows that, in male roe deer, hair cortisol concentrations are higher at the end of the hunting season than at the beginning. However, the hunting season also overlaps the mating season, so it’s impossible to tell whether roe deer are stressed by hunting or by mating-associated aggression and territorial behavior.

As far as I can tell, no one else has looked into chronic stress in hunted animals? Come on, guys. Jordan Hampton can’t do everything.

Conclusions

Wild-animal welfare advocates should oppose some forms of hunting. Animals shouldn’t be hunted with helicopters or dogs; they shouldn’t be chased for hours; they shouldn’t be trapped; I’d even argue against the use of battue. But stalking— which is the most common form of hunting—presents no serious direct welfare issues.

Looking at these studies, I start to ask myself whether wild-animal welfare advocates should actively support stalking, in at least some circumstances.

Unfortunately, studies almost never compare hunted animals to animals that died from a cause totally unrelated to humans. We can make some reasonable guesses about the relative welfare impacts of different ways that humans kill animals, but we can say very little about whether the average animal killed by a hunter experiences a more or less pleasant death than the average animal who dies from predation, disease, injury, parasitism, or starvation.

So what do we know?

The best resource I know on the causes of wild animal death is this from the Wild Animal Initiative. Predation is by far the most common non-hunting cause of death for both wild birds and wild mammals of all ages. (Presumably this is because sick or malnourished animals tend to be killed by predators before they die of illness or starvation.) We know very little about how much suffering is caused by the average death by predation. It seems unlikely to me, however, that predation is consistently a more pleasant death than being shot. If I had to pick, I personally would choose to be shot rather than eaten by a lion.

In ungulates, shooting injuries generally resulted in lower cortisol levels than did vehicle collisions, injury, disease, and entanglement in nets or fences, all relatively common causes of death for ungulates. Shot rabbits have lower levels of cortisol than rabbits caught through falconry. If you assume that falconry is sort of like predation, then it seems like shooting is less stressful than predation. Similarly, hunting with dogs is quite stressful, and it seems sort of like predation.

Nevertheless, certainly at least some animal deaths are more painful than stalking. People often reject vaccinations, predator removal, supplemental feeding, and other wild-animal welfare interventions because these interventions will increase animal populations to an unsustainable level and cause more suffering in the long run. But—at least sometimes—it seems to me that we could do these interventions and then kill the excess animals through stalking.

Some animal advocates would object that we should instead control wildlife populations through contraception. I am a huge supporter of wildlife contraception. But, right now, wildlife contraception is expensive, which means that it will only realistically be used in the most photogenic and charismatic of species. Mass wildlife contraception is simply not practical any time soon. Not only will people stalk animals for free, they will pay for the privilege. Stalking is so extraordinarily cost-effective that I think it’s a mistake to rule out its use as part of a comprehensive wild-animal welfare management plan.

Again, many forms of hunting present serious wild-animal welfare issues. And it is legitimate to be opposed to killing all animals, even if the animal experiences far less suffering than they would have if you didn’t kill them. But some forms of hunting clearly don’t cause much if any animal suffering, and I think many animal advocates should reconsider their opposition.

1

Of course, if you think it’s morally wrong to kill animals, you would want to not employ hunting as a management tool.

2

You can read the “wild animals plausibly have lives worth living” case here and the negative case here.

3

Remember this doesn’t necessarily mean that the animal actually dies instantaneously, just that the animal fell down and didn’t move.

item.title: Some thoughts on sexual harassment
item.content:encoded:
I.

Autism and social awkwardness don’t generally cause you to sexually harass people.

Here I’m talking about the unambiguous, uncontroversial, clear examples of sexual harassment. I’ll talk about the gray areas a bit later.

A boss asks out their employee, or a hiring manager asks out someone they’re considering for a role, or a mentor asks out their mentee. Someone asks out someone they know to be in a monogamous relationship. Someone approaches someone they don’t know crudely with a sentence like “nice tits.” Someone repeatedly asks someone else out, even after they’ve been clearly rejected. Someone grabs someone else’s breasts without their consent, or rubs their genitals on someone else without their consent.1

Now, is it possible that someone somewhere in the entire history of autism has sexually harassed someone in this sense, out of a sincere misunderstanding, because they’re autistic? Yes. It is not uncommon among autistic preteens and teenagers, who don’t yet know how to handle the new emotions of sexual attraction.2 Some autistic people are severely affected in a way that makes them struggle with even clearly communicated social norms—although I am skeptical that anyone who has this problem winds up being a boss, a hiring manager, or a mentor. It’s too obviously disqualifying.

Nevertheless, these are not confusing or ambiguous social norms. “You are not allowed to touch people without their consent” is a social norm taught explicitly to two-year-olds. “You are not allowed to ask people out if you are their employer, mentor, or considering them for a job” is generally covered, explicitly, in employee sexual harassment training. If you have managed to get through life without anyone explicitly telling you that you shouldn’t hit on people in monogamous relationships or tell complete strangers they have nice tits, consider this me telling you this fact. You’re welcome.

The world is full of confusing social norms; dating and relationships, even more so. These are not the confusing ones.

Indeed, autistic people I know are vastly more likely to make the opposite error: to become so self-effacing romantically and sexually that they never express romantic or sexual interest in anyone, and end up loveshy.

In general, sexual harassment is caused by:

  1. A person believes incorrect things about dating in general (“women secretly like it when you crudely compliment them”) or about this situation in specific (“that person is so into me that they want me to hit on them even though I’m their boss”).

  2. A person knows they’re coercing someone else into sex or a relationship, or knows that they’re making someone uncomfortable, and is doing that on purpose because they want to.

Now, you might assume that #1 is a thing autistic people do, because it involves misunderstanding social situations. It is mostly not. Autistic people like following clearly laid out rules for social interaction. “My illegible social intuition says I can override the clearly laid out rules for this social interaction and it’ll be fine” is an allistic social problem.

I think this misunderstanding is common for two reasons.

First, a lot of shy awkward people feel nervous about the possibility of accidentally sexually harassing someone. If you’re a decent person, it can be hard to understand why anyone would want to coerce people into a relationship or make people uncomfortable. And if you tend to be diffident and unassertive, it’s hard to imagine how someone could have no social skills disability and still be so delusional as to think that a monogamous person they just met wants to cheat on his spouse with them. So you end up asking yourself “why would I do this if I were in this person’s shoes?” and the answer you come up with is “I was profoundly confused about the basic norms of social interaction, because somehow I had gotten to the age of 35 without anyone telling me you’re not supposed to hit on people in monogamous relationships.” Because you’re scared that you might be making an equally grave mistake, you want to treat sexual harassers with a level of kindness and sympathy they don’t deserve.

Second, some people are sexual harassers or apologists for sexual harassers. They benefit from a system in which they’re held to low standards. If you’d like to get away with hitting on your employees, then of course you’re going to conjure up some kind of social-skills disability that leaves you unable to understand you’re not supposed to hit on your employees, but mysteriously still leaves you able to handle every other part of being a boss.

I urge shy awkward people who have a knee-jerk sympathetic reaction to sexual harassers to reconsider their choices. I understand why you do; I’ve been there. And, without meaning to, you are providing cover to predators—predators who are very likely to victimize people like you, shy awkward people who don’t understand social norms, because those people are easy to victimize. Have more solidarity for your own side than for the predators using you as a human shield.

II.

But there is the gray area, right.

Sometimes you can talk about sexuality (in a scientific way, or a joking shitposty way, or as gossip) at a party. Sometimes you can give people sexualized or romantic but not crude compliments, like “you have beautiful eyes” or “your legs look fantastic in that skirt.” Sometimes you can hold someone’s hand, or put your arm around their shoulder, or caress them, or play with their hair, or ask to do those things. Sometimes you can hit on people while you are drunk. Sometimes you can say perfectly neutral things, but communicate with your body language and tone of voice that you really, really want to fuck someone. Sometimes you can ask people if they’re going to Folsom next weekend. Sometimes you can ask people out!

No one except three radical feminists and four purity-culture weirdos wants a community where all of these things are unacceptable always in every circumstance. But all of these things have some chance of making people uncomfortable. And it’s… you know, bad? To make people uncomfortable?

And, realistically, if (conventionally attractive) women are continually having to fend off men asking to hold their hand or telling them they have beautiful eyes or subtexting their desire to fuck, they’re not going to want to go to your events. Your community is going to have a gender ratio that’s absolute shit.

Some people who don’t often get sexual attention (straight men, or less conventionally attractive straight women, or less queerly attractive queers) find it confusing why sexual attention would be a bad thing. But it makes sense! Imagine being hit on by someone you don’t find attractive at all (maybe someone of the wrong gender or orientation for you). It can be awkward. You are worried about letting them down gently and letting them save face. You are worried about not leading them on. You are worried about making them feel unattractive or unwanted. And since women tend to be socialized to be people pleasers and not to make a fuss, they often feel all of these worries much more acutely.

Now imagine getting hit on by someone who is larger and stronger than you and can beat you up, or someone who is more popular than you and hosts all the cool parties, or someone whom you know to be mean and vindictive when they get mad, or even someone where you don’t know how popular or how vindictive they are. Suddenly you’re worried about rejecting this person in a way that doesn’t make them mad or make them hate you. You don’t want to be yelled at or insulted. You don’t want to quietly stop getting party invitations, or have nasty rumors spread about you. And—even if you live in a culture where people don’t violently attack each other—there is still that lizard-brain that thinks this is the savannah and you don’t want to piss off the person who can murder you with their bare hands.

I don’t mean this to say that it’s bad or wrong to ask people out even if you might get rejected. It’s not. Asking people out can also be a good thing, because it can lead to romantic love and sex and friendship and babies and mutual support in times of trouble and growing old together still as in love as the day you met. Even if someone turns you down, they’re often happy and flattered to be asked! But, you know, “I don’t want to deal with delicate social interactions where I have to be careful with other people’s feelings” is also a natural, understandable desire.

I have thought about this a lot, as a Giver of Dating Advice. It is difficult to target your dating advice to the right demographic. Some people need to be advised to be bolder; other people need to be advised to be less bold. Some people need the advice “it isn’t an unthinkable moral horror to mistakenly make someone feel uncomfortable”; other people need the advice “before you say something, you need to think about how it might make other people feel.” Some people need both at once!

And there isn’t a single objective right level of boldness this margin is too narrow to contain. You can be bolder, without making anyone uncomfortable, if your community’s norms welcome sexual boldness. If you are attractive. If you are good at reading people and backing off when they give subtle signs of discomfort. If you come off as well-meaning and friendly and chill. If you tend to flirt with people who aren’t often flirted with but would like to be. If you’re white, or cis, or don’t have body language associated with neurodivergence.

Many of these are unfair! Some of them are oppressive! It’s still true.

I have mostly erred on the side of recommending boldness, because in my experience meeting my readers you guys all tend to be way too shy.

Also, being meek doesn’t always make women comfortable either. I have observed in several male-dominated spaces that conventionally attractive women get swarmed by a dozen men, all of whom clearly want to date and/or fuck her, but none of whom ever make this fact explicit enough that she can turn them down. This is unpleasant if you’re the center of the swarm and would like to have normal conversations without navigating the risk of hurting the swarm’s feelings or giving them false hope. My thought process here is that, if men instead make their desires more explicit and get rejected, they will swarm less and women will be more comfortable in the long run.

But… there is a risk, when I give this advice, that I’m giving it to entirely the wrong people. That some people are going to hear me say “be bolder, ask people out, don’t worry too much about making people transiently uncomfortable, we should all be more normal about sex and stop treating it as inherently taboo” and interpret me as saying “you should talk about sex whenever without paying attention to whether other people feel grossed out or embarrassed. You should tell every woman you think is pretty that she’s pretty regardless of circumstances or her likely feelings. Every conversation can have sexual subtext if you try hard and believe in yourself.”

III.

Some straight men ask a lot of women out. Like, a lot of women. Like, every woman they know and find minimally attractive.

This behavior:

  1. Even in the best of circumstances, makes some women feel unhappy, either because they didn’t like having to turn the guy down or because they don’t like being hit on by a man who would just as happily go out with anyone else with boobs.

  2. Is very effective for getting laid.

I don’t think this behavior, like, is evil or makes you a bad person, as long as you take no for an answer and avoid actual sexual harassment; I quite like some people who do it (although I also generally advise them to cut it out if the topic comes up). But it sure does make you obnoxious at parties. If more than a few guys are nonstop spamming out flirtation, an event can become unpleasant for every woman there.

But there’s not a hard line between good and bad behavior here, right? It’s not like the International Union of Feminists and Allied Women’s Groups have ruled that men can ask out no more than one woman per week, unless he can provide four reliable witnesses testifying that he has refrained from flirtation for at least three months previous. If you hit on more women, you are more likely to find someone who wants to have sex with you, making you and her happy (yay!). You also annoy more women and, if you’re indiscriminate enough, make more women feel like they’re primarily valuable as a validation dispenser and self-cleaning Fleshlight (boo!). You also burn the commons for other men, who are more likely to be assumed to be spamming out flirtations at every woman that moves (boo!).

When do the negatives outweigh the positives? Uh, shit, I don’t know. Probably listen if your friends tell you to hit on fewer women? Definitely listen if you’re at a con and conference staff tells you to hit on fewer women? But if your friends think spamming out flirtations is fine (because they’re friends with you so they probably think your behavior is fine), and if your behavior isn’t violating conference policies because you avoid outright harassment or aren’t at a con in the first place, then ????

Like, it would be one thing if this behavior were Definitely Bad, the way it’s bad to hit on your employees, and we could just ban it. But I don’t know how to think about people whose behavior improves their own lives, improves the lives of some other people, and often harms third parties. I would urge them to have good judgment, I guess? But “have good judgment” is almost uniquely terrible advice. If your judgment is bad enough, you always think you have good judgment.

I guess the economist solution is to tax it. Every time a straight guy hits on someone he has gotta pay $5 into the fund and at the end of the month we take the money and buy all the women and enbies ice cream.

IV.

I’ve been mostly talking in generalities here, because I want this post to be useful to people who aren’t embroiled in the topic du jour. But there is one point I do want to make specifically about Red Means No, the consensual nonconsent orgies organized by rationalist and sexologist Aella.

I have seen many claims that effective altruist and rationalist women feel ambient social pressure to go to Red Means No because of all the excellent networking there. As far as I can tell, the networking at Red Means No is… not… that great?

People I know are divided into two groups:

  1. [very small group] “Yay! Red Means No is fun! It makes me happy that I can go to it.”

  2. [extremely large group which includes me] “You couldn’t pay me enough money to go to Red Means No. Fortunately, this is a completely optional activity and I face no consequences whatsoever from refusing to attend.”

This is not because people I know are universally chill, emotionally stable people who trust that the quality of their work will show regardless of who their friends are. I have been subjected, quite against my will, to an enormous amount of discussion of the coworking space Constellation, who works there, who is trying to work there, who used to work there but doesn’t anymore, who has a real office and who is consigned to trying to find an empty call booth from which to take meetings, what criteria Constellation staff is using to make all these determinations, why Constellation staff should use alternate criteria that give the speaker a real office, etc. etc. From this, I conclude that Constellation is useful for networking and Red Means No isn’t.

There are some people who work in AI safety who attend Red Means No, but almost everyone who attends Red Means No doesn’t work in AI safety. Other effective altruist cause areas are even more poorly represented. “Some people who work in AI safety attend this event” is an honor that Red Means No shares with any number of recurring dinners, craft nights, singing nights, hiking clubs, SCA wars, D&D groups, niche freeform roleplay communities, rock climbing groups, Burning Man camps, and Starcraft guilds. Hell, I meet a bunch of the AI safety people I know by taking my kid to other children’s birthday parties, and I wouldn’t conclude from this that the AI safety community is pressuring everyone into having babies.

The majority of people at Red Means No are not rationalists. They are kinky people who enjoy a particular form of edgeplay BDSM, in a safe context, among other people who are enthusiastic about this form of edgeplay BDSM. Not all events founded by a rationalist have majority rationalist attendees. We can talk to non-rationalists, you know. It’s not illegal.

Furthermore, Red Means No is not very large. Even if all five or ten AI safety advocates who sometimes attend Red Means No took a solemn oath to only network with people they meet at sex parties, you could network with literally thousands of other people working in AI safety. In the real world, you could also network with these people the 362 days a year they aren’t attending a niche controversial sex party.

I say this not to defend the honor of AI safety. If I actually thought that women in AI safety were being expected to attend orgies for professional networking purposes, I would be the first to object. But I’m worried that if a bunch of people are saying “you have to be okay with consensual nonconsent orgies to be a woman in AI safety” then the vast majority of women—who, like the vast majority of people, couldn’t be paid enough money to attend a consensual nonconsent orgy—are going to select out of working in AI safety. Why bother if you’re always going to be locked out of the highest echelons of the community because of your sexuality? Why bother if men only see you as, not just a sex object, but a sex object for a single, specific, relatively rare, disturbing-to-many-people kink?

Like, the guest list for Red Means No is (quite rightly) private. You can’t ever know that people aren’t attending consensual nonconsent orgies. If some people are making this claim very confidently, it makes sense that a lot of people would believe it, because they have no access to evidence that it’s bullshit. But as far as I can tell it is bullshit?

The AI industry, effective altruism, and the rationality community surely have enough problems with gender dynamics already. We don’t need to be making up problems with which to terrify women newly entering the community.

V.

Here’s an interesting little game to play about your favorite group of people well-known enough to have cancel mobs whipped up about them. I always find the results enlightening, especially if the cancel mob purports to be feminist or acting in the interests of women or trying to make women welcome.

  • What percentage of the people cancelled are women? How does this compare to the overall demographics in the group?

  • Do women get cancelled for different things than men do? In particular, do men get cancelled for things like “is a rapist” or “embezzled huge amounts of money” while women get cancelled for things like “made a tasteless joke” or “wrote a story I think is Problematique” or “I don’t like her vibe”?

  • Are there men who are doing the exact same thing the woman is doing without being bothered?

  • If a man is cancelled, are the women around him cancelled for not disowning him quickly or fervently enough? Do these cancellations take into account any reasons she might have for not disowning him (e.g. financial dependence, child custody, abuse)? Does the same thing happen if the genders are swapped?

  • If a man does something wrong, do people condemn him less enthusiastically than they condemn a nearby woman who failed to stop him?

  • What percentage of the women cancelled are Bad? That is, what percentage are queer, or trans, or gender-non-conforming, or sexually promiscuous, or sex workers, or noticeably fat, or unphotogenically mentally ill, or otherwise doing something Our Culture Believes It Is Bad For Women To Do?

  • What percentage of the people cancelled are queer men, trans men, gender-non-conforming men, or nonbinary people assigned male at birth whom everyone’s misgendering?

  • What is it called, legally, when you target someone for harassment based on their sex, perceived sex, or behavior that doesn’t match the expected behavior for their sex?

You can take this too far. Women and nonbinary people can be bad actors too, and I have seen women and nonbinary people claim that they’re being cancelled because of misogyny when they were actually being cancelled for theft, blatant plagiarism, sexual assault, or stirring up harassment mobs. If your identity shields you from scrutiny, bad actors will take advantage of that. You always need to consider the merits of every individual case on its own and not just assume that members of some demographic are safe.

And, indeed, someone can legitimately be a victim of misogynist harassment and also be a bad actor who is hurting people. You must be able to both condemn misogynist harassment and condemn whatever bad stuff the victim actually did.

But, you know, I do recommend taking a step back and thinking about what percentage of the rage directed at this person is because of something they actually did wrong. Ask yourself: what percentage of this rage is clearly because— as a few completely random examples with absolutely no connection to any specific person— she’s a woman who openly talks about sex, or a woman who sells sex, or a woman who is edgy and courts controversy even though she knows perfectly well only men are supposed to do that, or a hot woman who doesn’t take many showers and therefore dares to be Not Pleasing To This Specific Man’s Boner?

Huh. Wow. Fascinating. What a bizarre coincidence. I am sure this means nothing.

Read Hot Allostatic Load, guys.

(and is also clearly the largest-scale victim of SlutCon-related sexual harassment)

1

This is actually called “sexual assault” or “sexual battery” and it is illegal.

2

Some of my readers are cringing right now remembering their own bad behavior in seventh grade.

item.title: Effective altruism and PR
item.description: I. The “effective altruists should be more concerned about PR” brigade has been out in full force on X recently.
item.content:encoded:
I.

The “effective altruists should be more concerned about PR” brigade has been out in full force on X recently. For example, the Center for New Liberalism (which is generally EA-sympathetic) wrote:

Now, FTX and Situational Awareness (presumably not the essay but rather the hedge fund that collapsed [ETA: had a really bad quarter but is still going, thank you Andrew Hunter]) are both a fair cop. I too wish I had a magic button that would stop effective altruists from starting hedge funds.

“The movement is the modern day Christianity” is I think a reference to this tweet from Scott Alexander—

—which is a JOKE. J O K E. JOKE.

There has not been a movement in the history of the world that managed to keep everyone in it from making edgy jokes in publicly available fora. If the socialist movement could take over multiple countries in spite of Oscar Wilde opining that we need socialism because poor people are ugly of body and soul, I believe in effective altruism’s ability to survive Scott Alexander’s X feed.

But I think veganism, AI welfare, and polyamory are more serious issues, and I want to talk through why I think effective altruists should continue to care about AI welfare, reduce animal-product consumption as much as is practical, and have whatever relationship style they prefer.

II.

Effective altruists were right(ish) about AI in 2015, but not because they had access to the world’s first effective Magic 8-Ball, or because a fairy appeared in a burst of sparkles and whispered in their ears while they were sleeping. Effective altruists were right(ish) about AI in 2015 because we had particular thought processes and habits of mind, which gave us the right answer on this question.

No one who warned about existential risk from AI was doing so because they were concerned about popularity, public relations, and appealing to the Median Voter. People who worried about those things gave focus-grouped and poll-tested statements about how we need to make sure that all Americans learn to code so that we can be Prepared for The Economy of the Future in which we have automated all jobs except programmer—and they were all wrong.

As far as I can tell, the argument here is “so, you guys were right years before everyone else about what is shaping up to be one of the most important political and ethical issues of our time. You were right even though everyone was laughing at you and calling you apocalypse cultist weirdos and saying that you needed to shut up about it for PR purposes. By vocally caring about this issue before anyone else, you wound up with a lot of ability to influence it, hopefully for the better. So now, when people are laughing at you and calling you anti-human cultist weirdos and saying that you need to shut up about different things for PR purposes, you should definitely listen and take me seriously!”

Here are two things that, in my opinion, are far more obviously true than “AI risk is a big deal” was in 2015:

  • Factory farming is an ongoing moral atrocity of incomprehensible scope under every mainstream system of morality. The only reason it survives is that people are avoiding thinking about it because they want to eat tasty and inexpensive animal products. If you cast a spell that made everyone actually get what was happening on factory farms, industrial animal agriculture would end tomorrow.

  • We are very confused about consciousness and moral patienthood. We are also very confused about how modern AI models work. Modern AI models straightforwardly pass the Turing Test. If you showed a modern LLM to someone back in 1995, they would say “oh, this is a conscious computer like C-3PO.” I’m not saying LLMs are definitely conscious, but if you dismiss the question of AI moral patienthood completely out of hand, you are being the villain of iconic Star Trek episode The Measure of a Man.

By vocally caring about AI welfare and factory farming, effective altruists can potentially make progress on these important issues, and so save billions of farmed animals and digital minds from horrific mistreatment.

Look. Once you have already had an enormous victory for the cause of Think With Numbers and Expand Your Moral Circle and Be Prepared To Be Weird If That’s Where The Evidence Takes You, you shouldn’t abandon quantitative reasoning, moral circle expansionism, and the willingness to be weird. It’s time to double down! It’s clearly working!

III.

But polyamory?

I don’t think “everyone in effective altruism has a normal dating life” is going to do that much for public relations. Most people have bigger worries than San Franciscans’ scandalous dating lives (bit of a ‘dog bites man’ story, really). And the New York Post is clearly willing to run articles like “Daniela Amodei and her husband adorably talk through their life problems together using a council of stuffed animals” and “some women who work for METR have short hair.” Even if everyone in the effective altruism movement saved themselves for marriage and had vanilla missionary-position sex with the lights off, the people with a slavering hatred of effective altruists would find some other innocuous thing to be mad about. Like, these are the people who literally claim that effective altruists are starting cult compounds because many effective altruists have roommates.

At the same time, I don’t think most people who recommend “all effective altruists should become monogamous” are thinking clearly about how this is supposed to work. Let’s say that every effective altruist suddenly agreed that they should become monogamous for the sake of effective altruist PR:

  • An effective altruist woman is happily married to a man who isn’t an effective altruist, but who married her under the understanding that they’d be poly and who has absolutely no intention of closing the relationship. Is she supposed to divorce her husband?

  • An effective altruist man and an effective altruist woman are happily married, but he’s asexual and they agreed that she could have sex outside the relationship. Their relationship is happy, but he would be miserable having sex and she would be miserable being celibate for the rest of her life. Are they supposed to divorce?

  • Three effective altruists are married. Who gets divorced?

  • Four effective altruists are not married but are raising their children together. Are they supposed to split the children into two households, separating their children from their other parents and siblings?

  • Two high-earning effective altruists financially support their shared partner, who is disabled and can’t work a job. Are they obligated to throw him out on the street? (Perhaps they’re only obligated to stop having sex with him and not to stop financially supporting him. Which of “your sex life” or “your weird household financial relationship” is generally more obvious to the New York Post?)

  • A man’s secondary partner is a ridiculous workaholic who never takes breaks, so he’s her entire support network. Is he supposed to dump her? (Will we get a ruling from the Grand High Council of Effective Altruist Poobahs about exactly how emotionally intimate a relationship can be before you count as “polyamorous”?)

I can literally keep doing this all day.

Polyamory and monogamy are both sticky because people make commitments on the understanding that they will continue to have a certain relationship style, and switching relationship styles often means breaking your commitments. Of course, you can in serious situations break your commitments. If polyamory (or monogamy) is making you absolutely miserable, you are under no obligation to continue to do it just because your partners are expecting you to.

But in general if someone you love is relying on you to do something, you ought to do it! If someone has made life plans under the reasonable expectation that you would stay married to them, raise children with them, financially support them, or even just continue to be a loving presence in their lives, you are supposed to do that unless you have a really damn good reason not to. And “the New York Post might be mad at me” is not a really damn good reason.

It’s true that people who haven’t made any commitments could switch to being monogamous. But there are already a lot of monogamous effective altruists and it doesn’t seem to have stopped anyone from posting. As long as poly people are overrepresented in effective altruism, people are going to complain about polyamory in effective altruism. And the usual case is that people have made commitments that they’d have to break if they changed relationship style, because most of the time when people are in long-term loving relationships they make some kind of commitments to each other, and that doesn’t change if you’ve got more than one.

I am assuming here that everyone is magically convinced by the arguments. But in reality that would never happen; you’d have to set some kind of social norm. Can we just think concretely about what that means? What you’re saying is “your friends should tell you to break up with your girlfriend, who brings you joy and makes your life shine, if she happens to have a sex life Middle America would disapprove of, because the approval of random strangers is more important than love.”

Like. No? Fuck you? Watch more Hallmark Christmas movies and straighten yourself out.

IV.

Everyone who devotes their life to a claim that 99.9% of people think is ludicrous is a fucking weirdo.

First- and second-wave feminists were disproportionately lesbians (a sexual minority far more maligned at the time than poly people are today). John Woolman—one of the most prominent early abolitionists—spent much of his life wearing only bleached-white clothes because of his unusual interpretation of Revelation. You see this with weird ideas that have nothing to do with morality, too—for example, a founder of the Jet Propulsion Laboratory was a polyamorous Thelemite occultist who attempted to incarnate the Whore of Babylon with the help of L. Ron Hubbard. Over the long arc of intellectual history, effective altruists seem if anything unusually normal.

This is perfectly expected if you think about it. People who are willing to defy society’s norms in one way are also willing to defy them in other ways. If you’re the kind of person who says “women and men should be equal” or “slavery is a serious moral wrong” even though everyone makes fun of you, you’re also the kind of person who says “there’s nothing wrong with being gay” or “I should wear bleached white clothes at all times” even though everyone makes fun of you.

And moral and intellectual trailblazers are extremely high in Big Five Openness—that is, creativity, curiosity, and intellect. But people who are high in Big Five Openness also tend to be neophiles: they’re going to speak ancient Greek, take up circus arts, read all the classics of Ukrainian literature, try durian, learn to forage mushrooms, and (yes) have weird sex. And they tend to be tolerant, to value freedom, and to question tradition and orthodoxy. So you are far less likely to convince them that they ought to do something solely because everyone else is doing it or because society says it’s good.

Now, I’m not saying that you shouldn’t cut your hair and put on a suit if you’re going to testify before Congress. (Or buy a really good wig and put on lipstick, depending on gender.) Nor am I saying that you can’t be curious, intellectual, and creative and also an intolerant conformist who hates new things. While the facets of Big Five traits are correlated on a population level, individuals can be high in one facet and low in another. For example, all effective altruists are high in Altruism and low in Tender-Mindedness, even though these are both facets of Agreeableness and correlated in the general population.

I’m also not saying that people have to be poly to do good intellectual work. Many freedom-loving neophiles are monogamous, including effective altruist freedom-loving neophiles. The specific weirdnesses of the effective altruist community are mostly a historical accident. We could have just as easily all been furries.

But in general posts like the Center for New Liberalism’s are asking for fried ice. You can’t get groundbreaking moral and intellectual work without the kind of people who produce groundbreaking moral and intellectual work. Those people are individually kind of weird, and when you put a bunch of them in a group with each other their weirdness feeds on each other and they get really really weird. Fortunately, we as a society have solutions to this problem, like the existence of professional people wearing suits who can take the weirdos’ ideas and repackage them for general consumption. “Everybody stop being weird right now!” doesn’t work and has never worked and you should stop annoying me by calling for it.

item.title: Think concretely about effective altruist optics
item.description: I. I think, when you talk about effective altruist “optics” or “public relations” or anything like that, you should make a concrete claim like this:
item.content:encoded:
I.

I think, when you talk about effective altruist “optics” or “public relations” or anything like that, you should make a concrete claim like this:

[Specific person, demographic, organization, or group of organizations] should [take specific action], which I think will have [specific consequence] because [specific reason].

You should not make a claim like this:

Effective altruists should stop with the [vague concept I dislike] because it’s bad for the movement.

Here are some examples of concrete claims, some I agree with and some I don’t:

  • People who are taking meetings with politicians should dress in a professional manner, which I think will make the politicians take them more seriously because they’re signaling that they’re serious adults.

  • Effective altruist organizations should avoid seeming to endorse people associated with crypto, which I think will keep them from seeming to endorse fraudsters, because crypto is full of fraud and it’s safe to assume that most crypto people are fraudsters.

  • Eleos AI should shut down, which I think will make ordinary Americans more sympathetic to AI safety, because they will only be asked to believe that their chatbots are dangerous and not that their chatbots are dangerous and also people.

  • Polyamorous effective altruists should become monogamous, which I think will make the New York Post run less interesting attacks that are less likely to go viral, because normal people are way more interested in weird sex than they are in some female METR employees having short hair.

  • Effective altruist X users should stop making shrimp memes, which I think will make non-effective-altruist X users more sympathetic to animal advocacy, because the shrimp memes are setting a frame that caring about shrimp is weird and edgy when we should actually be normalizing caring about shrimp.

  • The Effective Ventures Foundation should not have bought an abbey for use as an event space, which I think would make the New York Post etc. less likely to smear effective altruists as out-of-touch elitists, because the Effective Ventures Foundation wouldn’t be giving the Post etc. a concrete and obvious example of effective altruism’s out-of-touch elitism.

  • Ozy should stop posting sex advice and effective altruism material on the same Substack, which I think would make Substack readers more sympathetic to effective altruism, because they would be less likely to associate effective altruism with having a weird sex life.

Here is an example of a thing you should not say:

  • Effective altruists need to care more about public relations! What with FTX, shrimp welfare, AI welfare, the abbey, and all the weird sex, of course normies aren’t going to take them seriously. Real consequentialists would understand that they need to make some simple sacrifices for the sake of appealing to normal people.

My first list is made up of specific proposals. You can consider the costs and benefits of each proposal, and then try to convince particular people that they should take particular actions. My second list is just a more elaborate way to say “Boo FTX, shrimp welfare, AI welfare, abbeys as event spaces, and weird sex!” I mean, by all means, boo FTX. But what are we supposed to do about it?

If you have a concrete proposal, then it raises questions like:

  • Does my proposal involve creating social norms in which people believe something for a reason other than “this thing is true”?

  • Does my proposal involve an unreasonable level of meddling in the private lives of consenting adults?

  • Does my proposal involve thousands of people universally maintaining a lie about some easily verifiable feature of reality?

  • Does my proposal involve thousands of people universally behaving well and not e.g. telling edgy jokes, getting in stupid arguments, or making poorly thought out posts on microblogging platforms?

  • Is my proposal, in fact, already happening?

  • Does my proposal only work if people who observably Just Make Shit Up about effective altruists all the time respond to it by going “oh, it looks like we were mistaken about effective altruists” and not “let’s Just Make Some More Shit Up”?

  • How accurate is my model of what people find off-putting or irritating? Do I have, like, polling data? Relevant personal experience? Or am I just pulling it out of my ass?

  • Is the group whose opinions of effective altruists I want to change actually paying enough attention to notice whether my proposal is put into action?

  • Is there, in fact, any reasonable path through which my proposal improves anything?

And I think if we address those questions, instead of shaming people for not being concerned enough about PR, we’d make a lot more progress towards a sensible approach to effective altruist public relations.

II.

I suspect that often “optics” or “public relations” actually means “I think this thing is bad, but I’m not really sure why I think this thing is bad, or I’m suspicious that I’m going to lose the argument if I try to say it’s bad on the merits, so instead I’m going to point to some other people who think it’s bad and say ‘if you do this thing, you’re going to make those people hate us.’”

Like, I very rarely see arguments from people who are like “shrimp and AIs are moral patients, but we can’t admit this to anyone because of public relations.” Or “the abbey was fine, but Effective Ventures shouldn’t have bought it because the whole situation looks really bad.” Or “crypto is the currency of the future, but effective altruists shouldn’t associate themselves with it because of PR.” Or “I personally am a huge fan of racism, but effective altruism needs to separate itself more clearly from racists because normal people hate racism.”

“Shrimp welfare is bad optics” is an argument almost exclusively made by people who think shrimp are tiny little swimming automatons. “Racism is bad optics” is an argument almost exclusively made by people who don’t like racists.

Now, I don’t think you should dismiss out of hand “I have a sense that this thing is bad but I’m not sure why.” Often, your intuition is correctly pointing out something fucked up. A lot of people got kind of bad vibes from FTX. The people who listened looked prescient and the people who said “well, I can’t point to anything specific that’s bad about FTX” provided cover for a fraudster. Your intuition is pretty smart, especially about monkey politics, and a lot of the time it’s correctly putting together weird illegible evidence that hasn’t entered your conscious awareness.

But similarly your intuition can be misguided. I think that’s what’s up with a lot of the debate about the abbey. It’s not that it’s wrong to buy an event space (and indeed almost no one who feels uncomfortable with the abbey feels uncomfortable with Lighthaven, an equally expensive space that happened to be a former hotel rather than a former abbey). But the abbey serves as a metonym for wider objectionable tendencies in the effective altruism movement. People have legitimate concerns about loss of frugality, about “sometimes spending more money is more cost-effective in the long run, or when you take into account time and energy costs” becoming “the most effective cause is that me and my friends have a nice time.”1 And their intuitions collect the entire jumble of objections to behavior that is individually Probably Fine or None Of Your Business but collectively A Bad Pattern, and then turn it into an objection to the concept of an event space in the UK.

And everyone (whether they’re articulate about their true objections or not) should be honest about what’s driving their discomfort. If your problem with shrimp welfare is that you don’t care about shrimp, or your problem with AI welfare is that you don’t care about AI models, you should say that, and then argue about what makes something a moral patient and whether shrimps or AIs have those properties.

It can seem more tempting to say “shrimp welfare is bad because it makes us look weird to normies” than “shrimp welfare is bad because it’s a waste of money because shrimp don’t matter morally.” But if you say the first thing, while believing that shrimp are moral patients, you’re essentially saying that it’s okay to suffocate sentient beings to death, when it was possible to cheaply prevent this, because if you say “hey, it’s bad to suffocate sentient beings to death” then people might think you’re weird.

And if your objections are still incoherent and hard to articulate, but your intuition won’t stop bothering you that something is wrong here, then it’s okay to say “this gives me bad vibes and I don’t know why.” If someone says “this gives me bad vibes and I don’t know why,” you shouldn’t press them to make a clear and unassailable argument about what exactly is wrong; you should listen and help them try to figure out what their objection is. In that way, we can figure out whether there actually is something wrong, instead of getting distracted by a stupid argument about PR that is no one’s real crux.

III.

A while ago, I was concerned that my Substack was bad for effective altruist public relations, because I’m weird and poly and queer and I sometimes write about sex. So I went and consulted some people I respect who are boring suit-wearing DC types about this question, and they made three points that I thought were very reasonable.

First, by far the worst thing that happened to effective altruist public relations was the involvement of prominent effective altruists in a multibillion-dollar fraud. If you are not personally doing a multibillion-dollar fraud, or promoting people who are doing multibillion-dollar frauds, probably your actions won’t affect effective altruist public relations that much.

Second, boring suit-wearing DC types are absolutely willing and able to throw weird horny San Franciscan types under the bus. Mostly they don’t bother, because even raising the topic creates too many connections between themselves and the weird horny San Franciscans.2 It is much more effective to say “I love Innovation, and also America, and National Security, and did I mention that I am a huge fan of America” and leave the topic of effective altruism to one side. But if it did come up they would be happy to distance themselves from me and I don’t have to do it preemptively.

Third, effective altruism benefits from a diverse influencer network. My readers aren’t the same as Scott Alexander’s or Andy Masley’s or Sarah Hastings-Woodhouse’s. A lot of my readers find Scott Alexander off-putting; a lot of Andy’s readers find me off-putting. That’s great! You can’t be convincing to one group of people without being off-putting to some other group. The best course of action—rather than trying to write inoffensive slop that persuades no one—is to have a diversity of writers, who are taking different approaches, including the approach where you sometimes write about weird sex.

The effective altruist content creator community has some obvious gaps, like “literally anyone who votes Republican.”3 But I can’t fill those gaps by being fake and inauthentic. If I were any good at being fake and inauthentic, I wouldn’t be a Substacker. I would move to DC and put on a suit and talk a lot about how much I love Innovation and also National Security and most of all America. But instead I am terrible at not saying what I think at all times regardless of public relations concerns, and so I should lean into this and be a Substacker and convince people who like their effective altruism with a side of Woke and Horny. And I should not worry about the people who are turned off by the Woke and Horny; it is someone else’s job to convince those people.

I think this is a more reasonable approach to effective altruist PR than the one provided on X and in various Substack comment sections.

1

I’ve written about this here and here.

2

In fact, the boring suit-wearing DC types are successful enough at distancing themselves that many people appear to sincerely believe that effective altruists don’t have any boring suit-wearing DC types. Surely if a group exists they would also produce viral Substack posts.

3

If you’re an effective altruist who votes Republican and who wants to start a Substack, email me at ozybrennan@gmail.com and I’m happy to give advice and answer any questions you have.

item.title: It isn’t always evil to ally with Steve Bannon
item.content:encoded:
Scott Alexander wrote:1

Some of the people working with the companies think there might be a deontologic bar against certain types of mass activism. The sorts of arguments that do well on LessWrong.com won’t give us landslide wins in national elections. That’s going to require things like working with Steve Bannon, working with Bernie Sanders, working with NIMBYs who hate data centers because they’re a thing that might be built in someone’s backyard (or by non-union labor), training TikTok influencers create short-form videos about the dangers of AI, and holding protests where we chant vapid slogans outside AI company headquarters. There are better and worse ways to do all these things, but once you lay out the welcome mat, you have limited control over who shows up - and every time someone tries to create the Peaceful Nonviolent Pause AI Movement Based On Peaceful Nonviolence For Peaceful Nonviolent People, it spends an inordinate amount of resources keeping out violent crazies who want to tag along.

I mostly like Scott Alexander’s discussion of deontological bars in this post, but I think it is absurd to claim that there is any deontological bar against working with Steve Bannon or Bernie Sanders. To the contrary, it is actively virtuous to work with Steve Bannon and Bernie Sanders.

In a democratic society, we resolve conflicts through the democratic process. We vote for elected officials. We donate to political campaigns. We contact our elected officials to lobby for policies we think are good. We protest bad policies. We try to persuade other people to agree with us about issues.

Democracy is great! For example, more democratic countries have better public services, which leads to better health, and this effect is likely causal. Democratic countries tend to be better run, with higher state capacity and lower corruption. And democracy reduces the risk of catastrophic government failures, most notably famines.

But the democratic process inherently involves working with people you strongly disagree with, people whose views you consider to be stupid or evil.

This is what the political philosopher John Rawls calls the “overlapping consensus”. In a liberal society, we aim to create policies that people with wildly divergent worldviews and ethical systems can all agree on—especially when we’re talking about our basic institutions and the principles that underlie them. I think that your views are evil, and you think that my views are evil, but we can both support free speech because we both agree that society is better when we can say our bit without having to go to jail.

The overlapping consensus requires that people support broadly similar public policies, but not necessarily that people are going to agree on them for the same reasons. A Catholic might support a welfare state because all humans are created in the image and likeness of God. I support a welfare state because I believe all sapient beings ought to have the natural preconditions to be able to pursue their own flourishing. A nationalist might support a welfare state because it makes people have more, healthier children and therefore we have a larger and more effective military. But we can all agree that the welfare state is good.

Rawls was talking about the basic institutions of a society: things like “do people have a right to privacy?” and “should people be able to choose their own government?” and “should we make sure that the hungry are fed?” and “should fraud be illegal?” But I think the overlapping consensus is also a useful framework for thinking about more specific policies. The Mormons, a national security hawk who cares a lot about soft power, and I don’t necessarily agree on why PEPFAR is a great idea, but we all agree that it is.

You ideally want basically everyone in a society to agree on the right to vote, or the right to free speech, or the validity of a welfare state—you want as many people as possible to buy into the fundamental structures of public life and the state. The overlapping consensus around something like PEPFAR can be weaker. But I still think it’s helpful to think about what people with wildly divergent views can agree on.

I think a lot of “bipartisan”, “moderate”, “centrist” types agree with my points about the overlapping consensus in principle, but implicitly assume that you only have to bargain with, you know, reasonable people. Alice might believe that we should reduce the deficit, while Bob thinks we should lower taxes to spur growth, and Eve thinks we should expand the welfare state to reduce child poverty. But Alice, Bob, and Eve all read economics papers for fun and agree that we should have a free, equal, wealthy society that does well on all of Our World In Data’s charts. Ultimately, we’re all technocrats together.

But in fact the whole idea of an overlapping consensus is that you’re forming a consensus with people who have very different worldviews and ethical systems from you. That is, people whose views you find repugnant, people who seem stupid or evil to you, people with whom you agree about nothing except this one issue.

The feminist author Bernice Reagon wrote an excellent article called Coalition Politics: Turning the Century, which I recommend everyone read. She writes:

I feel as if I’m gonna keel over any minute and die. That is often what it feels like if you’re really doing coalition work. Most of the time you feel threatened to the core and if you don’t, you’re not really doing no coalescing.

I personally feel less threatened and more like I want to take a very long shower. Different people!

If you disagree with someone but think they’re reasonable and understandable, they probably agree with you about a lot of fundamental worldview and values stuff, even if you disagree about tax policy or whatever. If someone actually disagrees with you in a deep way, you will probably look at them and say “I don’t know whether I’m more shocked by your ethical myopia or your lack of connection to basic reality.” And if you are incapable of building a bridge to those people, regardless of which narrow policy points you agree on, you’re not really doing no coalescing.

The opposition to the Save Our Bacon Act—which would have overridden states’ ability to regulate welfare standards for animal products sold within their borders—got a crucial boost from MAGAs who believed a bizarre theory about Save Our Bacon being a Chinese plot to destroy American family farmers.2 I, uh, I don’t feel great about those people being on my side? In fact, the thought of allying with them makes me feel gross? But if I’m coalescing I don’t get to be happy about the entire coalition.

I don’t have to agree with the MAGAs about anything other than Save Our Bacon. I certainly don’t have to signal-boost their batshit theory. But if I had a MAGA Congressperson who worked against Save Our Bacon, I would call them and thank them. And if by some strange misadventure I wound up in Congress, I would work with my colleagues to defeat the bill, not complain that it should have been defeated by a coalition that was less stupid.

AI safety is a particularly good area in which to build coalitions because “humanity should not go extinct” is a moral claim with approximately 100% agreement. It easily outperforms something as controversial as “people should have the right to vote.” No matter how stupid or evil you think someone is, they almost certainly agree with you that it would be bad if everyone on Earth died and humanity went extinct. “AI companies should be legally forbidden from developing an advanced AI until it has been conclusively shown that that AI won’t kill everyone” is an issue that unites Steve Bannon and Bernie Sanders and Eliezer Yudkowsky and me. It is the most overlapping of overlapping consensuses. And there’s nothing deontologically wrong with acting like it.

1

Here you can see how good I am at responding to posts in a timely manner.

2

You see, American family farmers all produce high-welfare animal products [citation needed] and mistreatment of animals is strictly a big Chinese corporation thing.

item.title: The DBT guide to intense negative emotions
item.description: This is a guide for handling intense negative emotions, based on dialectical behavior therapy.
item.content:encoded:
This is a guide for handling intense negative emotions, based on dialectical behavior therapy. Dialectical behavior therapy was developed for chronically suicidal people and people with borderline personality disorder. While it has shown some usefulness in treating other mental health conditions, I’m not confident it would work for most people. But if you’re dealing with emotions you can’t handle, give it a try and see what happens.

Note that if you finish a step and you’re happy, then you can stop at that step. No need to continue to problem-solving if you’re perfectly cheerful about the situation once you’ve had a snack.

Thing of Things is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber.

Step one: triage. Are you in a crisis situation of some kind? That is, are you suicidal, self-harming, consuming drugs or alcohol to excess, screaming insults at people, breaking your possessions, or otherwise making obviously self-destructive decisions?

If you are in crisis, the first step is to calm yourself down enough that you can do the rest of the steps. Some techniques that people find useful include:

  • Regulating your nervous system: do intense exercise, muscle relaxation, or deep breathing. You can also stick your face in a bowl of cold water for about thirty seconds.

  • Enjoying pleasant physical sensations: eat some cake, look at a beautiful painting, pet a cat, listen to a favorite song, etc.

  • Distracting yourself: call a friend, read shitty fanfiction, cook dinner, play with your kid, program something, etc.

    • If you’re doing this, do something that makes you feel better, not something that makes you feel worse. Comedies are usually better than tragedies. Ask your friend to tell you about their day, instead of explaining everything you’re upset about. Doomscrolling is Right Out.

    • Often, you’ll feel better if you do something that helps other people. This doesn’t have to be anything big or super impactful (looking at you, effective altruists)—doing your housemate’s chore, bringing soup to a friend, or holding a friend’s baby are all good.

  • Changing your thought patterns: pray (if you’re religious), double numbers as high as you can go, recite poetry, visualize a peaceful place like a beach or a library, focus on your present-moment sensations, say encouraging words to yourself like “I can get through this,” remind yourself of the important reasons that you’re doing this horrible-but-necessary task, compare yourself to people in worse situations.

    • Comparison didn’t work for me for a long time because thinking about people in worse situations made me sad. However, I have found it useful, when I’m frustrated about my job, to remember that, as many abolitionists were Spiritualists, Frederick Douglass had to do abolitionist movement-building by attending seances. No matter how bad my day has been, I remind myself that I didn’t additionally have to go to a seance for work purposes, and that makes me feel better. Try it!

Of course, it is possible to use more than one technique at the same time. Many techniques work in multiple ways: for example, baking cookies might be distracting in the moment, helpful to others who will eat the cookies, and an enjoyable sensory experience. Different techniques work for different people, and if you’re regularly in crisis it’s worth experimenting.

If you are in crisis regularly, or if you anticipate a predictable crisis in the future, I can’t emphasize enough the importance of making a LITERAL PHYSICAL LIST OF TECHNIQUES THAT WORK, ON PAPER and then posting it somewhere you will see it when you’re in crisis. (Or several somewheres.) It is much, much, much easier to follow a written plan than to come up with your own plan on the fly.

Step two: deal with obvious physical causes of distress. Are you hungry? Thirsty? Did you miss your meds? Are you sick or in pain or in uncomfortable surroundings? Did you get four hours of sleep last night? Fix any of these you realistically can. If you can’t—you have untreatable chronic pain, you’re in a meeting and can’t leave to grab a snack, it’s late in the day and taking a nap would fuck up your sleep schedule—then consider whether you should triage like in step one until you can meet your physical needs, or move on to the next step.

Step three: figure out what you are feeling and what caused it. Sometimes this is obvious and then you can skip to the next step. But sometimes you just feel Bad and you don’t know why. Feelings can also disguise themselves as other feelings. For example, when I’m mad at myself for failing to do something I should do, I often get angry at other people for not rescuing me from my own problems by doing it for me. When I love someone and want to spend more time with them, I often feel guilty about not being good enough for them.

To figure out what you’re feeling, try observing what’s going on. Journaling or talking to a wise and honest friend can help. What are your body language and tone of voice like? What physical sensations are you feeling? What thoughts keep going through your head? What was happening when you first started feeling the intense emotion?

The most important thing to observe is what the emotion makes you want to do. An emotion is a motivation towards action, so all emotions come with an impulse to do something. Fear makes you want to run away and hide; anger makes you want to attack your enemy or defend yourself; sadness makes you want to seek comfort; guilt makes you want to apologize and repair the harm you did; love makes you want to spend time with the person you love. For me, the easiest way to work out what I’m feeling is to figure out what impulses I’m having, and then extrapolate from that what the emotion is.
