Step four: remind yourself that the situation is what it is. There are things you can control and things you can’t control. You can control: the actions you take in this present moment. You can’t control: your past actions, your feelings, your desires, other people’s thoughts or feelings or desires or actions, your health, the health of your loved ones, the weather, the traffic, the policies of bureaucratic institutions, AI, American electoral politics. Some of these you can influence, through the only thing you can control (the action you take in this present moment). But they are all determined by many factors outside of your control.

The economist Emily Oster says there is no secret option C. You can meet potential partners on the dating apps, you can meet them off the dating apps, or you can stay single. You can breastfeed, formula feed, maybe scramble to get donor milk, or let your baby starve. You can quit your job or stay at your job. You can go to the party, get work done, go to bed, or stay up all night on TikTok; you can’t do all four simultaneously.

Often, we are in situations where all of the available options suck. But you will not magically create a better option by refusing to make a decision, or complaining endlessly, or getting angry at the universe for being so inconvenient, or getting angry at yourself for not being clever enough to devise the secret option C, or pretending that the secret option C exists until everything explodes. You are in the situation you are in right now, and you have to make the best decision you can given what is actually true about the world.

Sometimes, other people who aren’t you have the thing you want—a good job, a loving spouse, children, a book contract, the ability to transition genders, whatever—so you’ll think “why don’t I have that? It’s not impossible by the laws of the universe!” But you can’t just wake up tomorrow and have a spouse or a book contract or a different lived gender. You have to take every one of the intervening steps from where you are right now to where you want to be: going on dating apps, drafting a book proposal, taking HRT. There is usually not an option where you teleport magically to your desired outcome, or you would have done it already.

It can help to remind yourself that your present actions are under your control. Often, when we feel intense negative emotions, the problem is less the situation and more that we feel completely helpless and powerless. But you can always control what you’re doing right now. A simple reframe from “I have to do option A because I have been forced into doing option A by a cruel and unfeeling universe” to “I have chosen to do option A because it is my best option, even though option A sucks and I would really prefer the secret option C” often makes you feel better.

If you struggle with this skill, I recommend Tara Brach’s excellent Radical Acceptance. Although Brach is a Buddhist, the strategies in this book work regardless of your religion.

Step five: stop yelling at yourself about how your feelings are stupid. Your feelings are not stupid. Your emotions are the natural result of specific past events. Your emotions might be an unreasonable response to whatever set you off, but you have that unreasonable response for some logical, understandable, non-stupid reason.

Say to yourself: “I’m hungry. Many people have a hard time keeping control of their feelings when they’re hungry.” “I blew up at my boyfriend unfairly because he reminded me of my awful ex, and I got scared that he would treat me the same way. It’s perfectly natural.” “I had an awful day, so it makes sense that I would burst into tears when it turned out I’d lost my phone. It was the last straw.” “It would be really bad if I couldn’t find a new job, so of course I’m scared I won’t.”

If you do this properly, you should feel a sort of relaxation and easing of tension. Even if the situation is still awful, you feel more able to cope with it. Instead of seeming like an unmanageable whirlpool of despair you flinch away from, the bad situation feels like a set of specific concrete events that you can do something about. In some cases, acknowledging that your feeling is not stupid can even get rid of the negative feeling entirely. I find that this happens when the thing I want is primarily social. It’s not that I want to get my way about the living room layout, it’s that I want to feel like my preferred way of organizing the living room has merit. If I reassure myself that my way of organizing the living room is also fine, then I can cope with it being arranged differently.

If you don’t believe yourself when you say this, you can ask for sympathy from the wise and honest friend you found in step three.

Step six: check whether your feeling makes sense. This is a very important step. Many times, people assume that intense negative emotions are always irrational. In reality, people often feel bad because bad things are happening. Often, when you’re angry at someone, it’s because they’re actually being mean to you. Often, when you feel socially rejected, it is because your alleged “friends” actually don’t like you very much. Often, when you feel guilty, it’s because you actually did something that goes against your moral values.

My favorite technique for checking whether my feeling makes sense is to write down what happened in a bland, factual style. Don’t include any predictions about the future, emotionally charged language, inferences about what other people are thinking, or “should” statements. Aim to write only what you can observe with your senses, not the interpretations that you are applying to your observations. “My friend looked off into the distance and then started talking about movies,” not “my friend was bored and distracted and then changed the topic to something he actually cares about.” (Or “my friend said in a loud voice that I was ugly and disgusting,” if that’s what happened.) Once a factual description of what happened has been written down, it’s usually clear whether the story you’re telling yourself is what actually happened, or whether the facts admit of an alternate explanation.

Another useful technique is to think about what the absolute worst-case possible outcome is. Then, consider what you would do in the absolute worst-case possible outcome. I have spent an enormous amount of time feeling anxiety or guilt or anger about things where, upon contemplation, the absolute worst-case possible outcome was fine. Like “I would have to have an awkward conversation with someone” or “I would be out $200” or “I would spend an afternoon at the DMV.” Or something that seems disastrous isn’t that disastrous when I think about it: “I might lose all my friends—but anyone who would stop being my friend over that is an asshole that I’m better off without.”

It’s also helpful to get concrete about the absolute worst-case possible outcome because of what Cliff Pervocracy wrote in this post:

[K]nowing that there’s something horrible behind a door is terrifying. Once you open the door, it’s ruined. Even if it’s a really terrible thing behind that door, even if it’s a six-foot cockroach, any horror you feel is going to be mixed with relief. “Oh, thank God, it’s just a six-foot cockroach. It could’ve been a sixty-foot cockroach.”

If you think about the absolute worst-case possible outcome and how you would cope with it, then you often feel a sense of relief. The absolute worst-case possible outcome is just a six-foot cockroach. It is not an infinitely horrible doom pit forever. Infinitely horrible doom pits forever aren’t real.

Step seven: if your feeling doesn’t make sense, do opposite action. To do opposite action, you do the opposite of what the emotion is urging you to do. For example, if you’re scared, you should put yourself in the scary situation. If you’re angry, you should be kind to the person you’re angry at. If you feel guilty, you should repeat the action you’re guilty about. If you’re sad, you should go out and do fun things without seeking reassurance or comfort. If you’re in love with someone you shouldn’t be in love with, you should avoid them and stop daydreaming about the glorious future where you have a happy relationship.

If your emotion has some more specific desire associated with it, do the opposite of that. For example, if you want to ask everyone over and over again for reassurance that you’re a good person, you should instead go for a walk by yourself and then start a conversation about Interview with the Vampire.

You can tell that you’ve picked the right opposite action because it feels horrible and impossible. Ideally, even as your rational mind predicts this is going to be fine, every part of you should be screaming “you want me to WHAT?” That’s the kind of juicy opposite action that causes you to stop feeling these problematic intense emotions in the long run.

Note that it is only a good idea to do opposite action if your emotion doesn’t make any sense. If you are afraid of going to a party, but everyone will be kind to you, then you’ll learn that the party is nothing to be afraid of and going to parties will get easier. If you’re afraid of spiders, and you touch a harmless spider, then you’ll learn that spiders won’t hurt you and being around spiders will get easier. But if the party is actually full of people who will make fun of you or push your boundaries, or if the spider is actually going to bite you and send you to the hospital, your fear will get worse. Obviously! You’ve just taught yourself that there’s something to be afraid of.

Step eight: if your feeling does make sense, do problem-solving. If you have intense negative emotions because there is something actually bad in your life, you can’t fix the problem by changing your emotions. You have to solve the problem.

If someone is cruel or controlling, you can’t and shouldn’t solve your anger by telling yourself your feelings make sense or tricking yourself into thinking they’re good to you or being kinder to them or trying to understand their point of view. You need to stop spending time with a cruel, controlling person. Similarly, if you feel guilty because you did something that goes against your moral values, then it won’t help to try to convince yourself that it’s fine and certainly won’t help to do it again. You need to stop doing things that go against your values. If you’re sad because your cat just died, you shouldn’t try to repress your sadness. You should cry and let your friends comfort you.

It’s often helpful to be creative about what counts as a good solution to a problem. For example, let’s say you have an untreatable chronic illness that leaves you with two or three good hours a day. It’s normal to grieve. But you can think specifically about what makes your life worth living: maybe you particularly value spending time with your family, or going out in nature, or consuming art, or helping others. Then you can try to think about how you can fit as many of those things as possible into your two or three hours a day—even if it means deliberately deprioritizing other things, like housework. You can also try to figure out how to fit some of those things into your bad hours: maybe you can snuggle a loved one during bad fatigue hours and so spend time with your family anyway. You won’t end up with a life as full as able-bodied people’s, or as you would have hoped, but you can find a life that’s okay and that isn’t consumed with grief for what you can’t have.

Or maybe someone is awful but you have to put up with them (they’re your coworker at a job you otherwise love, or a close friend of your best friend, or the other parent of your child). Maybe “success” doesn’t look like never talking with this person. Maybe success looks like using coping techniques like “grey rock” and “broken record” to avoid conflict and set boundaries. Maybe success looks like lining up a support network who will let you complain to them and who thinks you deserve better. Maybe success looks like getting yourself to believe “that person’s negative opinion of me is because they’re an asshole, not because I did anything wrong. I’m okay.”

Often, the solution to a problem is a greyed-out option. You could fix your problem if you do something that people just don’t do. If you quit your horrible job, or got on meds, or got off meds, or moved to a different city, or told people “no,” or asked people out, or bought the silly frivolous thing that makes you happy, or fired your therapist, or switched careers, or worked more flexible hours, or hired cleaners, or decluttered, or did things you actually like instead of things that you think will make other people think well of you.

Sometimes, the path to the thing you want involves moving away from the secret option C. You want a healthy, committed romantic relationship with someone who loves you and treats you well, but you’re in a situationship with someone who is mean to you. You would prefer the secret option C where she suddenly decides she loves you and wants to be kind to you and spend the rest of her life with you. Breaking up with her means admitting that the secret option C will never happen, so you stay stuck.

If you are persistently, intensely unhappy about a situation, that situation is not tenable for you. It doesn’t matter if it would be tenable for someone else, or for you if you were a better person; you shouldn’t stay in situations that make you persistently, intensely unhappy. You must develop some plan for improving the situation.
